questions.text: The first hour: work-up, oxygen, nitrates and first drugs

steps.q:
**For the initial work-up of ACS, give:**
a The ECG requirement
b The monitoring requirement, and why
c The six blood tests sent with IV access
steps.a:
- 12-lead ECG **interpreted within 10 min**
- **Continuous ECG monitoring with a defibrillator available** - risk of VT / VF
**Bloods**
- Cardiac biomarkers | - Haemogram
- Electrolytes | - Lipid profile
- Renal and liver function | - HbA1c (if diabetic)
bank_lines: Marrow: Most early STEMI deaths (within 24 h, mostly in the first hour) are from VF — hence continuous monitoring and defibrillator-capable transport from first medical contact.

explain.intro: Step 1 starts at first medical contact. The ECG decides which pathway the patient enters, and the monitor is there because the first hour is when he is most likely to die. The one real question asks what kills STEMI patients before they reach hospital.
why: **12-lead ECG interpreted within 10 minutes.** ESC 2023 makes this Class I (B) at the point of first medical contact, and both ESC and ACC/AHA use the same 10-minute target. The ECG is what separates STEMI (go to reperfusion, MI-40) from NSTE-ACS (risk-stratify, MI-43); troponin is never awaited for a STEMI decision.

**Continuous ECG monitoring with a defibrillator available, because of the risk of VT/VF.** Acute ischaemia makes the border zone electrically unstable (re-entry around dying tissue, raised automaticity, potassium leak). Most early STEMI deaths, within the first 24 hours and mostly in the first hour, are from ventricular fibrillation, often before the patient reaches hospital. That is why transport from first contact must be defibrillator-capable.

**Cardiac biomarkers, haemogram, electrolytes, lipid profile, renal and liver function, HbA1c if diabetic.** Troponin (high-sensitivity, on the 0/1 h or 0/2 h algorithm) makes the NSTEMI diagnosis; the haemoglobin and platelets set bleeding risk before antithrombotics; potassium and magnesium matter for arrhythmia; creatinine sets drug doses and contrast risk; the lipid profile is most accurate when drawn early.
mimic: Early death in STEMI vs later death
First hours: VF (electrical). Days later: pump failure and mechanical complications (free wall rupture, VSD, papillary muscle rupture).
traps: “Most prehospital STEMI deaths are from cardiogenic shock or rupture”
They are from VF, mostly in the first hour; shock and rupture kill later.
decode: Commonest cause of prehospital death in STEMI? [Marrow]
Ventricular fibrillation.
Within what time must the first ECG be read after first medical contact? [pattern]
10 minutes.
explain.punch: Read the ECG within 10 minutes, because it chooses the pathway, and keep a defibrillator beside the patient, because the first hour of STEMI kills by VF.

steps.q:
**For hypoxaemia and symptom relief in ACS (ESC), give:**
a When oxygen is indicated, and its class
b When routine oxygen is NOT recommended, and its class
c Opioids - dose in the notes, and class
d The anxiolytic, and class
steps.a:
- SaO₂ **<90%** or PaO₂ **<60 mmHg** - **I, C**
- SaO₂ **≥90%** - **III, A** (no benefit)
- IV morphine **5-10 mg** - titrated IV opioids **IIa, C**; cut sympathetic drive and O₂ consumption
- Mild tranquilliser (usually a **benzodiazepine**) in very anxious patients - **IIa, C**

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Oxygen and symptom relief
explain.intro: Still in step 1: treating symptoms without harming the patient. One real question tests the oxygen threshold, which one in three got wrong by reflexively giving oxygen to a patient who was not hypoxaemic.
why: **Oxygen if SaO₂ <90% or PaO₂ <60 mmHg: Class I, C.** Below 90% the oxyhaemoglobin curve is on its steep part, so oxygen delivery to ischaemic myocardium falls quickly and correcting it helps.

**SaO₂ ≥90%: routine oxygen not recommended, Class III, A (no benefit).** Hyperoxia constricts coronary arteries and raises reactive oxygen species. DETO2X-AMI (about 6,600 patients with SpO₂ ≥90%) found no difference in 1-year death (5.0% vs 5.1%), and AVOID suggested larger infarcts with oxygen. The ESC text says SaO₂ >90%; the card’s ≥90% is the same rule in practice.

**IV morphine 5–10 mg, titrated IV opioids Class IIa, C; they cut sympathetic drive and oxygen consumption.** Pain drives catecholamines, heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand. The catch: opioids slow gastric emptying, so oral P2Y12 inhibitors are absorbed later and platelet inhibition is delayed (shown with ticagrelor in IMPRESSION). That is why opioids are only IIa and should be titrated, not given routinely.
**A mild tranquilliser, usually a benzodiazepine, in very anxious patients: Class IIa, C.** The aim is the same as with opioids: lower sympathetic tone.
mimic: SaO₂ <90% vs ≥90%
The same number flips the class: below it oxygen is Class I, at or above it oxygen is Class III.
traps: “Low-flow nasal oxygen at 2 L/min is harmless at SaO₂ 95%”
Any routine oxygen without hypoxaemia is Class III; the DocT key is to withhold it (66% right).
“Morphine is a Class I part of the ACS bundle”
It is IIa and delays oral P2Y12 absorption.
decode: ACS patient, SaO₂ 95% — which oxygen strategy? [DocT GT]
Withhold oxygen.
Below what saturation is oxygen indicated in ACS? [pattern]
SaO₂ <90% (PaO₂ <60 mmHg).
explain.punch: Oxygen only below 90%; above that it adds nothing and may harm. Opioids and benzodiazepines are IIa, and opioids slow the oral P2Y12 load.

steps.q:
**For sublingual nitroglycerin in ACS, give:**
a The dose and repeat schedule
b The four contraindications
c What relief of pain proves
steps.a:
- **0.4 mg** (0.3-0.6 mg) SL, every **5 min**, up to **3 doses**
- **Hypotension** • **tachycardia** • **right ventricular MI** • **recent phosphodiesterase-inhibitor use**
- **NOTHING** - does not confirm or exclude MI; biomarkers are needed
bank_lines: Marrow: Riociguat (soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator) is a nitrate contraindication alongside PDE-5 inhibitors: both amplify the NO–cGMP pathway, so a nitrate causes profound hypotension.

explain.intro: Step 1 again: nitrates relieve ischaemic pain but can collapse the circulation in the wrong patient, and their effect proves nothing about the diagnosis. Five real questions test exactly these two points, and both DocT questions were got right by fewer than half.
why: **0.4 mg (0.3–0.6 mg) sublingual, every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses.** Glyceryl trinitrate releases nitric oxide, raising cGMP in vascular smooth muscle; at low doses it is mainly a venodilator, so it lowers preload and wall tension (less oxygen demand), and it also dilates epicardial coronaries and collaterals. The notes’ ‘5 mg’ is a source error (card watch line).

**Hypotension, tachycardia, right ventricular MI, recent phosphodiesterase-inhibitor use.** Each of these turns preload reduction into shock. An RV infarct is preload-dependent: the failing RV needs a high filling pressure to push blood through the lungs, so venodilation drops LV filling and the pressure falls (give fluid instead). PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil within 24 h; tadalafil within 48 h) block cGMP breakdown, so a nitrate causes profound hypotension; riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, acts on the same pathway and is also a contraindication. ESC adds marked bradycardia, and ACC/AHA use SBP <90 mmHg (or ≥30 below baseline) and HR <50 or >100.

**Nothing: relief does not confirm or exclude MI; biomarkers are needed.** Nitrates relax all smooth muscle, so oesophageal spasm also eases, and an MI may improve partly. The diagnosis comes from the ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponin.
mimic: Nitrate in hypertensive acute heart failure vs nitrate in RV infarct
Lowering preload rescues the congested LV in hypertensive AHF; it collapses the preload-dependent RV infarct.
Unstable angina vs oesophageal spasm with a normal ECG and negative troponin
Until serial hs-troponin and risk stratification rule out ACS, unstable angina is the working diagnosis; spasm is a diagnosis of exclusion.
traps: “Hypotension 10 minutes after nitroglycerin in inferior STEMI is a medication reaction”
46% chose this. The nitrate unmasked a preload-dependent RV infarct: it is cardiogenic shock (key B). Check right-sided leads (V4R) before nitrates in inferior STEMI.
“Chest pain relieved by nitroglycerin, normal ECG, negative troponin → oesophageal spasm”

DocT keys spasm (33% right), but the key is debatable: nitrate relief proves nothing, and with a single negative troponin unstable angina is the classic answer. If the stem says serial troponins are negative and ACS is ruled out, pick spasm; otherwise pick unstable angina.
“Hypotension after a nitrate is only a PDE-5 inhibitor problem”
Riociguat (sGC stimulator) does the same; Marrow keys it.
decode: Inferior STEMI, aspirin + nitroglycerin + morphine, BP falls to 60/30 in 10 min — why? [DocT QBank]
Cardiogenic shock from an RV infarct unmasked by preload reduction.
Inferior STEMI, hypotension, clear lungs, normal LV — next step? [Marrow]
Normal saline bolus; no nitrates.
Hypotension after SL nitrate — which drug interacted? [Marrow]
Riociguat.
Chest pain relieved by nitroglycerin, normal ECG, negative troponin — most likely? [DocT QBank]
Keyed oesophageal spasm; the defensible answer is unstable angina until serial troponins rule out ACS.
explain.punch: A nitrate lowers preload, so it is dangerous wherever preload is holding the pressure up: hypotension, RV infarct, and any drug that already floods the NO–cGMP pathway. Whether it relieves the pain tells you nothing.

steps.q:
**For early drug therapy in ACS, give:**
a Aspirin loading dose
b The second antiplatelet
c The statin and dose
d IV beta-blocker - indication, agent, contraindications
steps.a:
- **300 mg** on arrival
- **P2Y12 inhibitor** loading dose - prasugrel, ticagrelor or clopidogrel
- **High-dose statin** - atorvastatin **80 mg** →
- Tachycardia + SBP **>120 mmHg** **IV metoprolol** (limits infarct size); avoid in **heart failure** and **hypotension**
bank_lines: Marrow: IV β-blocker contraindications in ACS: signs of HF or low output, LVEF ≤40% with shock risk, PR >240 ms or 2nd/3rd-degree block, hypotension (SBP <120 with risk factors), active asthma/bronchospasm, and age >70 with tachycardia >110 (COMMIT: more cardiogenic shock).

explain.intro: The last part of step 1 is the drugs given on arrival, before the reperfusion decision. The one real question tests the contraindications to an IV beta-blocker, which are wider than the card lists.
why: **Aspirin 300 mg on arrival.** Aspirin acetylates platelet COX-1 irreversibly, so thromboxane A2 production stops for the life of the platelet; a loading dose works within minutes, faster still when chewed. ESC 2023 gives 150–300 mg oral (75–250 mg IV); ACC/AHA use 162–325 mg chewed. Both are right in their own system.

**A P2Y12 inhibitor loading dose: prasugrel, ticagrelor or clopidogrel.** Aspirin blocks only one platelet activation pathway; ADP acting on P2Y12 is the other main amplifier, so the two together (DAPT) are needed. Timing of this load is a separate question (MI-50: routine pretreatment is not recommended in NSTE-ACS).

**High-dose statin: atorvastatin 80 mg.** High-intensity statin is started early regardless of cholesterol (Class I); the benefit is plaque stabilisation and LDL lowering, and early starting improves long-term adherence.

**Tachycardia with SBP >120 mmHg: IV metoprolol (limits infarct size); avoid in heart failure and hypotension.** Slowing the heart lowers oxygen demand and lengthens diastole, so less myocardium dies (METOCARD-CNIC, before primary PCI); ESC 2023 gives it IIa A in PPCI patients without acute heart failure and with SBP >120. The danger is a patient whose output depends on his heart rate: in COMMIT early IV metoprolol caused excess cardiogenic shock, mostly in the first day and in those with heart failure, low pressure or tachycardia. Contraindications therefore go beyond the card: signs of HF or low output, risk of shock (age >70, HR >110, SBP <120), PR >240 ms or second/third-degree block, and active asthma or bronchospasm.
mimic: Tachycardia from ischaemia and pain vs compensatory tachycardia of low output
The first is a target for a beta-blocker; the second is what keeps a failing heart’s output up, and blocking it causes shock (COMMIT).
traps: “The only contraindications to an IV beta-blocker in STEMI are heart failure and hypotension”
Heart block (PR >240 ms, second/third degree), bronchospasm and high shock risk are also contraindications; Marrow’s ‘all except’ question keys ‘none of the above’.
decode: Contraindications to a beta-blocker in STEMI — all of the following except? [Marrow]
None of the above: HF/low LVEF, heart block, hypotension and asthma all count.
Aspirin loading dose in ACS (ESC)? [pattern]
150–300 mg oral; ACC/AHA 162–325 mg chewed.
explain.punch: Aspirin, a P2Y12 load and a high-dose statin go in early for everyone; an IV beta-blocker only for a tachycardic, normotensive patient with no failure, no block and no bronchospasm.

questions.text: The clock: primary PCI or lysis

steps.q:
**Give the ESC time targets for STEMI:**
a FMC to ECG and diagnosis
b Diagnosis to wire: the cut-off for choosing primary PCI
c Diagnosis to wire: presenting at a PCI centre
d Diagnosis to wire: transferred patients
e Diagnosis to lytic bolus
f Lysis to evaluation of efficacy
g Lysis to angiography
steps.a:
**Interval** | **Target**
FMC → ECG and diagnosis | **≤10 min**
Diagnosis → wire: choose PPCI over lysis if achievable | **≤120 min**
Diagnosis → wire, at a PCI centre | **≤60 min**
Diagnosis → wire, transferred | **≤90 min**
Diagnosis → lytic bolus | **≤10 min**
Lysis → evaluate efficacy | **60-90 min**
Lysis → angiography | **2-24 h**

explain.intro: Step 2 is the clock that decides reperfusion. Myocardium is lost with every minute of occlusion, and three real questions turn on one number: whether the wire can cross within 120 minutes of diagnosis.
why: **FMC → ECG and diagnosis: ≤10 minutes.** The clock for reperfusion starts at diagnosis, so delay here pushes everything else.

**Diagnosis → wire: choose PPCI over lysis if achievable within ≤120 minutes.** Primary PCI opens about 90% of arteries and has less intracranial bleeding than lysis, but its advantage is lost if it comes too late; 120 minutes is the delay at which lysis given now is roughly as good. This is a decision threshold (Class I, A), not a target.
**Diagnosis → wire at a PCI centre: ≤60 minutes.**
**Diagnosis → wire, transferred: ≤90 minutes.** Transfer adds time, so the target is looser; the targets are what a system should achieve, not cut-offs for choosing.

**Diagnosis → lytic bolus: ≤10 minutes.** If lysis is chosen, its benefit falls steeply with time, so it must not wait (ideally pre-hospital, MI-52). In the American system the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline sets FMC-to-device ≤90 minutes (≤120 minutes with transfer) and lysis when PCI will take more than 120 minutes; its door-to-needle goal of ≤30 minutes comes from the 2013 ACCF/AHA STEMI guideline and the AHA ACS algorithm.
**Lysis → evaluation of efficacy: 60–90 minutes.** By then a successful lysis has resolved ST elevation by ≥50%.
**Lysis → angiography: 2–24 hours.** This is the routine angiography after successful lysis (MI-42).
mimic: 120 min vs 90 min
120 is the decision threshold between PPCI and lysis; 90 is the target for transferred patients.
traps: “Transfer for PCI regardless of delay” with an expected 160-minute delay
Beyond 120 minutes lyse first (77% right); PCI follows anyway.
“Thrombolysis” in a STEMI at a PCI-capable centre
When PCI is available within 120 minutes it beats lysis; the 95%-right question keys primary PCI.
decode: Anterior STEMI, door-to-balloon expected 160 min — best initial management? [DocT QBank]
Immediate thrombolysis before transfer.
Inferior or anterior STEMI, troponin up, no delay mentioned — treatment? [DocT QBank]
Immediate primary PCI.
explain.punch: Ask one question at diagnosis: can the wire cross within 120 minutes? If yes, primary PCI (aim 60 or 90 minutes); if no, lytic bolus within 10 minutes.

steps.q:
**Route the STEMI strategy clock:**
a The first decision after diagnosis
b The ≤120 min path
c The >120 min path, and its first time point
d When reperfusion is judged, and the "no" branch
e The "yes" branch, and its window
steps.a:
- **Time to PCI?**
- **Primary PCI** - alert and transfer to a PCI centre; wire crossing by 90 min
- **Fibrinolysis** - bolus within **10 min**, then transfer to a PCI centre →
- At **60-90 min**: reperfusion criteria met? **No** → **RESCUE PCI**
- **Yes** → **routine PCI strategy at 2-24 h**
bank_lines: DocT Recall25: Stent thrombosis presenting with ST elevation is a STEMI: load DAPT (aspirin + P2Y12) with anticoagulation and send for immediate primary PCI. Lysis works poorly on platelet-rich stent thrombus; heparin alone or beta-blockers are not reperfusion.

explain.intro: Step 2 as a flow chart. This is the most asked card in the deck (ten real questions): almost all are the same decision, PPCI if timely and lysis if not, plus two on stent thrombosis, which is a STEMI and goes to the lab.
why: **Time to PCI?** The first and only decision after a STEMI diagnosis is whether the wire can cross within 120 minutes (MI-40). Distance, transport and lab availability all feed into it.

**Primary PCI: alert and transfer to a PCI centre; wire crossing by 90 minutes.** Bypassing the emergency department and taking the patient straight to the lab saves time; at a PCI centre the aim is 60 minutes.

**Fibrinolysis: bolus within 10 minutes, then transfer to a PCI centre.** Lysis is a bridge, not the end of treatment: every lysed patient is moved to a PCI centre immediately (ESC Class I, A), because a third or more fail to reperfuse and some re-occlude.

**At 60–90 minutes: reperfusion criteria met? No → rescue PCI.** Failure means less than 50% ST resolution, ongoing pain, or haemodynamic or electrical instability (MI-42). A second dose of lytic does not help.

**Yes → routine PCI strategy at 2–24 hours.** The lysed artery still sits on a ruptured plaque with residual stenosis; angiography within 2–24 hours lowers re-infarction without the bleeding of immediate PCI on a fully lytic state.
mimic: Stent thrombosis vs post-PCI pain without new ST change
New ST elevation in the stented territory is stent thrombosis, a STEMI: back to the lab. Pain with an unchanged ECG gives time for other causes.
Rescue PCI vs routine PCI after lysis
Rescue: lysis failed, go now. Routine: lysis worked, go at 2–24 hours.
traps: “Immediate transfer for primary PCI” when the PCI centre is 150 km or 4 hours away
The delay is well over 120 minutes: lyse, then transfer (NEET 2025, Marrow).
“Intravenous nitroglycerin, observation or echo first” for new ST elevation after a stent
Only 48% chose repeat angiography. Acute stent thrombosis is a STEMI; anything else delays reperfusion.
“Thrombolysis” for stent thrombosis
Platelet-rich stent thrombus responds poorly to lysis; load DAPT, anticoagulate and do urgent PCI (NEET 2025).
Marrow’s ‘PCI at 3–24 h’ after lysis
Its explanation says 3–24 h; ESC says 2–24 h. The answer, lysis then transfer, is unaffected.
decode: STEMI, PCI centre 150 km away (or 4 h, or door-to-balloon 160 min) — next step? [NEET 2025] [Marrow] [DocT GT]
Thrombolysis, then transfer to a PCI centre.
STEMI with PCI available — most appropriate treatment? [DocT QBank]
Primary PCI.
DES 2 months ago, sudden anterior ST elevation — immediate management? [NEET 2025]
DAPT with urgent PCI.
New chest pain and ST elevation hours after a successful circumflex stent — next step? [DocT GT]
Urgent repeat coronary angiography.
explain.punch: One decision: PCI within 120 minutes, or lyse within 10 and transfer. After lysis, failure means rescue PCI now and success means angiography at 2–24 hours; stent thrombosis is a STEMI and goes straight back to the lab.

next?

**after successful lysis**

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → STEMI without on-site PCI: pharmaco-invasive strategy
explain.intro: Step 4 begins with the commonest ACS decision outside a PCI centre. Primary PCI is better than lysis only if it can be done quickly; the card gives the time limit and what follows lysis.
why: **If PCI cannot happen within 120 min of diagnosis → lyse (within 10 min of diagnosis; door-to-needle ≤30 min).** Beyond about 120 minutes of delay the advantage of PCI over lysis is lost to the extra myocardium that dies waiting (ESC 2023). Lysis works best early, when the thrombus is fresh and fibrin-poor, and is given within 12 hours of symptom onset. ESC targets the bolus within 10 minutes of the diagnostic ECG; the AHA target is door-to-needle within 30 minutes.

**Transfer for angiography 2–24 h after lysis (mini test: 3–24 h). Not before 2–3 h (bleeding peak).** Lysis opens the artery in about half to two thirds of patients but leaves the ruptured plaque, so routine early angiography prevents re-occlusion; within the first hours the lytic state makes arterial puncture and PCI more likely to bleed and gave no benefit (facilitated PCI).

**Below 50% ST resolution at 60–90 min, ongoing pain or instability → immediate rescue PCI.** ST resolution is the bedside marker of tissue reperfusion; failure to resolve by half means the artery is probably still closed. Repeat lysis is not effective.
mimic: Rescue PCI vs pharmaco-invasive PCI
Rescue: lysis failed, go now. Pharmaco-invasive: lysis worked, angiography in 2–24 h.
traps: “Transfer for PCI regardless of delay” when door-to-balloon is 160 min
Lyse first (77% right); ‘regardless of delay’ applies to cardiogenic shock (CAR-18a).
“1 h” or “48 h” for angiography after successful lysis
2–24 h; the mini test answer was 12 h (34% right).
decode: Anterior STEMI, door-to-balloon expected 160 min — best initial management? [DocT QBank, 77%]
Immediate thrombolysis before transfer.
Anterior STEMI 1 h, nearest PCI centre 150 km away [NEET 2025 recall]
Thrombolysis.
explain.punch: If PCI cannot happen within 120 minutes of diagnosis, lyse within 10 minutes, then transfer for angiography at 2–24 h, or go for rescue PCI at once if ST elevation has not fallen by half at 60–90 minutes.

steps.q:
**For the timing of fibrinolysis, give:**
a When benefit is maximal
b What is preferred after 3 hours
c The latest symptom duration for lysis
d The target from diagnosis to bolus
e What the "2-24 h" window in the notes really refers to
steps.a:
- Within **2 hours** of symptom onset
- **PCI** preferred over fibrinolysis
- Up to **12 hours** - still effective, reduced benefit
- **≤10 min**
- The window for **angiography after SUCCESSFUL lysis** (MI-42)

explain.intro: Step 3: when lysis still works. No real question is linked; the card also corrects a mix-up in the notes between the lysis window and the post-lysis angiography window.
why: **Within 2 hours of symptom onset.** A fresh thrombus is fibrin-rich and loose; over hours it becomes organised and cross-linked, so lytics dissolve it less well, while the myocardium at risk is already dying. Lives saved per 1,000 treated fall steeply after the first 2–3 hours.
**PCI preferred over fibrinolysis after 3 hours.** As lysis loses effect with time, the mechanical approach keeps its patency rate, so PCI wins when it can be done within the 120-minute window.

**Up to 12 hours: still effective, reduced benefit.** ESC: lysis within 12 hours of symptoms if PPCI cannot be done in time (I, A). Beyond 12 hours the risk outweighs the benefit; late STEMI (12–48 h) goes to PCI (IIa, B).
**The window for angiography after SUCCESSFUL lysis (MI-42).** 2–24 hours is not a window for giving lysis.
mimic: Lysis window vs post-lysis angiography window
Lysis: up to 12 hours of symptoms. Angiography after successful lysis: 2–24 hours after the lytic.
traps: “Lysis is effective within 2–24 hours”
A notes error; lysis is for symptoms ≤12 hours.
decode: STEMI with 14 h of symptoms, no PCI nearby, pain settling — lyse? [pattern]
No; beyond 12 hours lysis is not indicated, transfer for PCI.
explain.punch: Lysis works best in the first 2 hours and not at all usefully after 12; 2–24 hours is the angiography window after lysis, not a window for giving it.

steps.q:
**When fibrinolysis is the reperfusion strategy, give:**
a When and where to start it
b The type of agent
c The adjustment for age ≥75
d The antiplatelet regimen
e Anticoagulation afterwards
steps.a:
- **As soon as possible** after diagnosis, preferably **pre-hospital** - I, A
- **Fibrin-specific** (tenecteplase, alteplase, reteplase) - I, B
- **Half-dose tenecteplase** - IIa, B
- **Aspirin + clopidogrel 300 mg**
- Continue **until revascularisation**

explain.intro: Step 3: how lysis is given. No real question is linked; the likely test is that the P2Y12 partner for lysis is clopidogrel.
why: **As soon as possible after diagnosis, preferably pre-hospital: Class I, A.** The benefit of lysis falls fastest in the first hours (MI-54); giving it in the ambulance saves the most myocardium.
**Fibrin-specific agent (tenecteplase, alteplase, reteplase): Class I, B.** They act mainly on fibrin-bound plasminogen, giving better patency than streptokinase.
**Half-dose tenecteplase: IIa, B.** Intracranial haemorrhage rises with age (MI-51).

**Aspirin + clopidogrel 300 mg.** ESC 2023 Class I, A. Clopidogrel is the P2Y12 inhibitor tested at the time of lysis (CLARITY, COMMIT); prasugrel has not been tested with lysis, and ticagrelor only when started a median of about 11 hours afterwards in patients under 75 (TREAT: no more major bleeding than clopidogrel). More potent platelet inhibition given with the lytic risks intracranial bleeding. Over 75 years, clopidogrel 75 mg without the 300 mg load.

**Continue anticoagulation until revascularisation.** ESC: until revascularisation, or for the hospital stay up to 8 days, Class I, A. Enoxaparin (IV bolus then subcutaneous) was better than UFH with lysis in ExTRACT-TIMI 25.
mimic: P2Y12 with lysis vs with PCI
Lysis: clopidogrel. PCI: prasugrel or ticagrelor.
traps: “Ticagrelor or prasugrel with tenecteplase”
Clopidogrel is the partner for lysis.
decode: STEMI being lysed: which P2Y12 inhibitor and dose? [pattern]
Clopidogrel 300 mg (75 mg if >75 years) with aspirin.
explain.punch: Lyse early, ideally pre-hospital, with a fibrin-specific drug (half-dose tenecteplase if old), add aspirin and clopidogrel, and anticoagulate until revascularisation.

steps.q:
**Give the dose of each fibrinolytic:**
a Streptokinase
b Alteplase
c Reteplase
d Tenecteplase, and the elderly adjustment
steps.a:
**Drug** | **Dose**
**Streptokinase** | **1.5 million units** IV over **30-60 min** →
**Alteplase** | **15 mg** bolus → **0.75 mg/kg** over 30 min (max 50 mg) → **0.5 mg/kg** over 60 min (max 35 mg)
**Reteplase** | **10 U + 10 U** boluses **30 min apart**
**Tenecteplase** | Single weight-based bolus: **30 mg** <60 kg, 35 mg 60-69, 40 mg 70-79, 45 mg 80-89, **50 mg** ≥90 kg; **HALF-dose if ≥75 y**

explain.intro: Step 3 turns to lysis itself. No real question is linked; doses are asked as recall, and the tenecteplase bands and its half dose in the elderly are the usual targets.
why: **Streptokinase 1.5 million units IV over 30–60 minutes.** Not fibrin-specific: it activates circulating plasminogen as well as clot-bound, so it causes systemic fibrinolysis and hypotension, and it is antigenic: antibodies form within days and persist, so it is not repeated (ACC/AHA: not within 6 months).

**Alteplase: 15 mg bolus → 0.75 mg/kg over 30 minutes (max 50 mg) → 0.5 mg/kg over 60 minutes (max 35 mg).** The accelerated 90-minute regimen; the maximum total is 100 mg, which a patient of 67 kg or more receives as fixed 15 + 50 + 35 mg. Its short half-life is why it needs an infusion.
**Reteplase 10 U + 10 U boluses 30 minutes apart.** A longer half-life allows two boluses.

**Tenecteplase: single weight-based bolus, 30 mg <60 kg, 35 mg 60–69, 40 mg 70–79, 45 mg 80–89, 50 mg ≥90 kg; half-dose if ≥75 years.** Tenecteplase is the most fibrin-specific and longest-acting, so one bolus suffices, which makes it the pre-hospital agent. In STREAM, intracranial bleeding in the elderly was 3 of 42 before the protocol halved their dose and none of 93 after it (non-randomised, hypothesis-generating); ESC gives half-dose IIa, B.
mimic: Streptokinase vs fibrin-specific agents
Streptokinase: systemic lysis, hypotension, allergy, cheap. Fibrin-specific agents: clot-bound plasminogen, bolus dosing, preferred (I, B).
traps: “Full-dose tenecteplase for an 80-year-old”
Half dose from 75 years (ESC ≥75). Do not confuse it with the clopidogrel rule after lysis, which drops the 300 mg load only above 75.
decode: Tenecteplase dose for a 72 kg patient aged 60? [pattern]
40 mg single bolus.
explain.punch: Tenecteplase is one weight-based bolus of 30–50 mg, halved from 75 years; alteplase is the 90-minute three-step infusion; streptokinase is 1.5 million units and not fibrin-specific.

steps.q:
**Sort the contraindications to fibrinolysis:**
a Absolute (eight)
b Relative (eight)
steps.a:
**Absolute** | **Relative**
Prior ICH or stroke of unknown origin - **any time** | **TIA** in preceding **6 months**
**Ischaemic stroke** in preceding **6 months** | Oral anticoagulant therapy
CNS damage, neoplasm or AVM | Pregnancy or within 1 week post-partum
Major trauma / surgery / head injury within **1 month** | Refractory hypertension (SBP >180 and/or DBP >110)
GI bleeding within **1 month** | Advanced liver disease
Known bleeding disorder (excluding menses) | Infective endocarditis
**Aortic dissection** | Active peptic ulcer
Non-compressible puncture in 24 h (liver biopsy, LP) | Prolonged or traumatic resuscitation
bank_lines: Marrow: Active diabetic haemorrhagic retinopathy is a relative contraindication to fibrinolysis; a previous MI is not a contraindication; CPR counts only if prolonged (>10 min) or traumatic.

explain.intro: Step 3: who must not be lysed. Five real questions test this list, often in PE or rural STEMI stems; the hidden difficulty is that different guidelines draw the stroke and surgery windows differently.
why: **Absolute: prior ICH or stroke of unknown origin at any time; ischaemic stroke in the preceding 6 months; CNS damage, neoplasm or AVM; major trauma, surgery or head injury within 1 month; GI bleeding within 1 month; known bleeding disorder (excluding menses); aortic dissection; non-compressible puncture in 24 h (liver biopsy, LP).** The common thread is a site that would bleed catastrophically (brain, aorta, a fresh wound) once fibrin is dissolved everywhere. Aortic dissection matters because it can mimic STEMI (inferior ST elevation when the flap involves the right coronary).

**Relative: TIA in the preceding 6 months; oral anticoagulant therapy; pregnancy or within 1 week post-partum; refractory hypertension (SBP >180 and/or DBP >110); advanced liver disease; infective endocarditis; active peptic ulcer; prolonged or traumatic resuscitation.** Here the risk is weighed against the benefit. Marrow adds active diabetic haemorrhagic retinopathy as relative; a previous MI is not a contraindication; CPR counts only if prolonged (over 10 minutes) or traumatic.
mimic: Ischaemic stroke vs TIA within 6 months
Same window, different class: stroke absolute, TIA relative.
traps: “Prior ischaemic stroke 5 months ago” or “surgery 2 weeks ago” offered beside a known AVM
Under the ESC list (this card) both are absolute too; the GT key is AVM (75% right) because it is absolute in every guideline. When several look absolute, pick the one no list disputes.
“SBP >180 mmHg” or “warfarin and aspirin” as absolute
Both are relative; previous haemorrhagic stroke is absolute (68% right).
“Only contraindicated if on anticoagulation” for massive PE with ischaemic stroke 2 months ago
Ischaemic stroke within 6 months is absolute in ESC PE and STEMI rules (71% right); stroke-lysis rules use 3 months.
decode: Absolute contraindication to thrombolysis in STEMI? [DocT QBank]
Previous haemorrhagic stroke.
Rural anterior STEMI, transfer 3 h — which is an absolute contraindication? [DocT GT]
Known arteriovenous malformation.
Massive PE with shock, ischaemic stroke 2 months ago — eligibility? [DocT GT]
Absolute contraindication.
Post-op day 2 MI with hypotension — what is NOT recommended? [Marrow]
Thrombolytic therapy (surgery within 1 month).
explain.punch: Lysis dissolves fibrin everywhere, so anything that would bleed into the brain, aorta or a fresh wound rules it out; brain lesions and prior ICH are absolute in every list, and stroke within 6 months is absolute but TIA is only relative.

parts.q: Contraindication to fibrinolysis in acute MI among the options? [Marrow]
parts.a: Active diabetic haemorrhagic retinopathy (relative); previous MI is not a contraindication.

steps.q:
**After fibrinolysis, give the action and class for:**
a Heart failure / shock
b Failed lysis - definition and action
c Successful lysis
d Recurrent ischaemia or re-occlusion
e What watchful waiting alone does
steps.a:
**Situation** | **Action** | **Class**
**HF / shock** | **Emergency** angiography ± PCI | I, A
**Failed lysis** | **RESCUE PCI** immediately - <50% ST resolution at 60-90 min, or instability, or worsening ischaemia | I, A
**Successful lysis** | Angiography ± PCI of IRA at **2-24 h** | I, A
**Re-occlusion** | **Emergency** angiography ± PCI | I, B
- Lysis + watchful waiting ↑ **re-infarction**; routine PCI after lysis reduces it

explain.intro: Step 3 follows the lysed patient. Lysis never ends the treatment; what happens next depends on how the patient looks at 60–90 minutes. No real question is linked, but the branches are the same ones MI-41 tests.
why: **HF or shock: emergency angiography ± PCI, Class I, A.** Shock after lysis means a large area is still ischaemic or a mechanical complication is present; only opening the artery or fixing the defect helps.

**Failed lysis: rescue PCI immediately — <50% ST resolution at 60–90 minutes, or instability, or worsening ischaemia; Class I, A.** ST resolution is a bedside marker of tissue reperfusion; under 50% means the artery is probably still shut.
**Successful lysis: angiography ± PCI of the infarct-related artery at 2–24 hours, Class I, A.** The plaque and residual stenosis are still there.
**Recurrent ischaemia or re-occlusion: emergency angiography ± PCI, Class I, B.**

**Watchful waiting after lysis raises re-infarction; routine PCI after lysis reduces it.** Trials of early routine angiography after lysis against an ischaemia-guided approach (such as CARESS-in-AMI and TRANSFER-AMI) found less re-infarction and recurrent ischaemia, without more bleeding.
mimic: Rescue PCI vs facilitated PCI
Rescue is for failed lysis. Immediate PCI on top of successful lysis (facilitated PCI) is not recommended: more bleeding, no benefit.
traps: “Successful lysis needs no angiography”
Watchful waiting raises re-infarction; angiography at 2–24 hours is Class I.
decode: Lysed anterior STEMI, ST resolution 30% at 90 min — next step? [pattern]
Immediate rescue PCI.
Lysed STEMI, ST resolved, pain-free — when angiography? [pattern]
Within 2–24 hours.
explain.punch: After lysis, failure or shock means the lab now, success means the lab in 2–24 hours; nobody is simply watched.

questions.text: Antithrombotics: what blocks what, and when

steps.q:
**Map each drug group to its target:**
a Aspirin
b Clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor
c Eptifibatide, tirofiban
d Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, fondaparinux
e UFH, enoxaparin
f Dabigatran, bivalirudin
steps.a:
**Drug** | **Target**
**Aspirin** | **Thromboxane A2** (COX)
**Clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor** | **P2Y12** ADP receptor
**Eptifibatide, tirofiban** | **GP IIb/IIIa**
**Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, fondaparinux** | **Factor Xa**
**UFH, enoxaparin** | **Xa and thrombin**
**Dabigatran, bivalirudin** | **Thrombin** (direct)
- GP IIb/IIIa: **bailout** only (no-reflow / thrombotic complication) - IIa, C
- Cangrelor: P2Y12-naive patients - IIb, A
bank_lines: DocT GT: Cangrelor is the only IV P2Y12 inhibitor — reversible, t½ 3–6 min, platelet function back within 30–60 min — so it bridges a recent-stent patient whose oral P2Y12 must stop for urgent surgery (BRIDGE). Eptifibatide and tirofiban block GP IIb/IIIa, not P2Y12.

Marrow + DocT GT: Eptifibatide inhibits platelets within ~15 min, t½ ~2.5 h, function recovers in ~4–8 h; renal dosing differs by drug: eptifibatide halved when CrCl <50 (contraindicated on dialysis), tirofiban halved when CrCl <30, abciximab none. Today GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors are bail-out drugs for no-reflow or thrombotic complications during PCI.

DocT GT: Aspirin IRREVERSIBLY acetylates platelet COX-1, so thromboxane A2 production stops for the platelet's life (7–10 days); absent aggregation to arachidonic acid confirms it. Recovery needs new platelets (~10%/day), so platelet transfusion reverses it for urgent bleeding. NSAIDs block COX-1 reversibly; P2Y12 blockers abolish the ADP response.

explain.intro: Step 6 maps every antithrombotic to the step of clotting it blocks; that map answers the reversal and bridging questions. Three real questions test it, and the card layer adds aspirin’s irreversibility and the GP IIb/IIIa timings.
why: **Aspirin: thromboxane A2 (COX).** Aspirin acetylates platelet COX-1 irreversibly, and platelets have no nucleus to make more, so thromboxane A2 production stops for the platelet’s life (7–10 days). An absent aggregation response to arachidonic acid confirms the effect. Recovery needs new platelets (about 10% a day), so urgent bleeding needs platelet transfusion. NSAIDs block COX-1 reversibly.

**Clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor: P2Y12 ADP receptor.** Cangrelor is the only IV P2Y12 inhibitor: reversible, half-life 3–6 minutes, platelet function back within about an hour. That makes it the bridge when a recent-stent patient must stop oral P2Y12 for urgent surgery (BRIDGE), and an option in P2Y12-naive patients during PCI (IIb, A).

**Eptifibatide, tirofiban: GP IIb/IIIa.** GP IIb/IIIa is the final common pathway, the fibrinogen receptor that links platelets, so blocking it stops aggregation whatever the trigger. Eptifibatide inhibits platelets within about 15 minutes, half-life about 2.5 hours, function back in 4–8 hours. Renal dosing differs: eptifibatide infusion halved when CrCl <50 mL/min and contraindicated on dialysis; tirofiban halved when CrCl <30; abciximab needed none. Today they are bail-out drugs for no-reflow or thrombotic complications during PCI (IIa, C).
**Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, fondaparinux: factor Xa.** The oral agents block Xa directly; fondaparinux does so indirectly through antithrombin.

**UFH, enoxaparin: Xa and thrombin.** Both work through antithrombin. UFH chains are long enough to bridge antithrombin and thrombin, so anti-Xa and anti-IIa activity are about equal; enoxaparin’s shorter chains act mainly on Xa (ratio about 3–4 to 1). Protamine fully reverses UFH, only partly enoxaparin.

**Dabigatran, bivalirudin: thrombin (direct).** They bind thrombin without antithrombin, so they also inhibit clot-bound thrombin and do not interact with platelet factor 4 (hence bivalirudin in HIT, MI-49).
mimic: Cangrelor vs eptifibatide/tirofiban as an IV bridge
Cangrelor replaces the oral P2Y12 blocker; GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors act on a different receptor and are bail-out drugs, not bridges.
traps: “Tirofiban or eptifibatide” as the IV bridge for a patient on clopidogrel needing surgery
They block GP IIb/IIIa, not P2Y12; cangrelor is the answer (80% right).
“Aspirin inhibits COX-1 reversibly”
Irreversibly; that is why its effect lasts the platelet’s life and transfusion is needed.
Abciximab
No longer marketed in most countries; it bound irreversibly. Eptifibatide and tirofiban remain.
decode: Recent stent, on aspirin + clopidogrel, needs urgent surgery — IV bridging agent? [DocT GT]
Cangrelor infusion.
On aspirin 81 mg, GI bleed, absent response to arachidonic acid — mechanism? [DocT GT]
Irreversible COX-1 inhibition.
Eptifibatide bolus + infusion — time to platelet inhibition? [Marrow]
About 15 minutes.
explain.punch: Aspirin hits thromboxane for the platelet’s life, the P2Y12 drugs hit ADP (cangrelor is the IV, reversible one), the GP IIb/IIIa drugs hit the final common pathway, and the anticoagulants hit Xa, thrombin or both.

steps.q:
**For the P2Y12 inhibitors, give:**
a Which are thienopyridines
b Which are preferred, and over what
c The prasugrel contraindication and age caution
d The ticagrelor caution
steps.a:
- **Clopidogrel** and **prasugrel**. Ticagrelor is **NOT** - a reversible, direct-acting agent (cyclopentyl-triazolopyrimidine)
- **Prasugrel or ticagrelor** over clopidogrel (superior efficacy); clopidogrel if unavailable / contraindicated
- **Prior stroke or TIA**; avoid in older patients
- Prior **haemorrhagic stroke**; liver disease
bank_lines: DocT GT: Ticagrelor causes dose-related dyspnoea in up to ~14% (PLATO) — sudden air hunger with normal SpO2, examination, ECG and CT — from adenosine accumulation (it blocks ENT1 reuptake); usually mild and self-limiting, not a reason to stop unless intolerable. The same adenosine effect causes ventricular pauses.

explain.intro: Step 6 begins with the second antiplatelet. Two real questions test the drugs’ side effects and contraindications, and both were got right by less than half: ticagrelor dyspnoea (30%) and prasugrel after TIA (49%).
why: **Clopidogrel and prasugrel; ticagrelor is NOT — a reversible, direct-acting agent (cyclopentyl-triazolopyrimidine).** Thienopyridines are prodrugs whose active metabolite binds P2Y12 irreversibly, so their effect lasts the platelet’s life. Clopidogrel needs two CYP steps (CYP2C19), so its effect is slow and variable; prasugrel needs one, so it is faster and stronger. Ticagrelor is active itself and binds reversibly, so its effect wears off in 3–5 days.

**Prasugrel or ticagrelor over clopidogrel (superior efficacy); clopidogrel if unavailable or contraindicated.** TRITON-TIMI 38 and PLATO showed fewer ischaemic events (PLATO also lower mortality), at the cost of more bleeding. Clopidogrel remains the drug with lysis (MI-52) and with oral anticoagulants.

**Prior stroke or TIA; avoid in older patients.** In TRITON-TIMI 38 patients with prior stroke or TIA had net harm, with more intracranial bleeding. At 75 years or more, or under 60 kg, prasugrel is generally not recommended; if used, the maintenance dose is 5 mg.

**Prior haemorrhagic stroke; liver disease.** Ticagrelor is contraindicated after any intracranial haemorrhage; it is cleared by hepatic CYP3A4, so the label contraindicates severe hepatic impairment and ESC advises against it (and prasugrel) in moderate-to-severe liver disease. Its other effects come from blocking adenosine reuptake (ENT1): dyspnoea in about 14% in PLATO (vs about 8% with clopidogrel), with normal saturation, examination, ECG and CT, usually mild and self-limiting; and ventricular pauses.
mimic: Ticagrelor dyspnoea vs pulmonary embolism or heart failure after MI
Ticagrelor dyspnoea has normal SpO₂, examination, ECG and imaging, and follows the drug; PE and HF do not.
traps: “Aspirin or metoprolol causes the dyspnoea” 12 hours after PCI with normal SpO₂, exam, ECG and CT
Only 30% chose ticagrelor; the adenosine effect is the cause.
“Clopidogrel, ticagrelor or cangrelor is contraindicated after a TIA”
Only prasugrel is (49% right).
“Ticagrelor is a thienopyridine”
It is a reversible, direct-acting cyclopentyl-triazolopyrimidine.
decode: Post-PCI patient on aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol, atorvastatin: breathless with normal SpO₂, ECG and CT — culprit? [DocT GT]
Ticagrelor.
ACS with a recent TIA, planned for PCI — which P2Y12 inhibitor is contraindicated? [DocT GT]
Prasugrel.
explain.punch: Prasugrel and ticagrelor beat clopidogrel; prasugrel is out after any stroke or TIA and in the old, ticagrelor is reversible and causes dyspnoea and pauses through adenosine.

steps.q:
**For anticoagulation during primary PCI, give the dose / class of:**
a UFH
b Enoxaparin
c Bivalirudin (routine, and in HIT)
d Fondaparinux
e Anticoagulation after the procedure
steps.a:
**Agent** | **Dose / use** | **Class**
**UFH** | Bolus **70-100 U/kg** - preferred, routine | I, C
**Enoxaparin** | IV **0.5 mg/kg** | IIa, A
**Bivalirudin** | Routine | IIa, A
**Bivalirudin** | **HIT** | I, C
**Fondaparinux** | **NOT** recommended - possible harm | III, B
- **Generally not** - limited to the periprocedural period

explain.intro: Step 6 again: the anticoagulant during primary PCI. No real question is linked; the classic test is that fondaparinux is harmful here although it is Class I in conservatively managed NSTE-ACS (MI-50).
why: **UFH bolus 70–100 U/kg: preferred, routine, Class I, C.** It is cheap, its effect can be measured in the lab (ACT) and protamine reverses it. With a GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor the dose is lower (50–70 U/kg).

**Enoxaparin IV 0.5 mg/kg: IIa, A.** ATOLL compared it with UFH in primary PCI: the primary composite narrowly missed significance (28% vs 34%, p = 0.07), but death, recurrent MI or urgent revascularisation fell (6.7% vs 11.3%) with similar major bleeding.

**Bivalirudin: routine IIa, A; in HIT I, C.** A direct thrombin inhibitor with a short half-life and less bleeding; ESC 2023 makes it an alternative to UFH with a full-dose infusion continued after PCI (that removed the excess early stent thrombosis seen in older trials). It does not interact with platelet factor 4, so it is the agent of choice in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

**Fondaparinux: NOT recommended, possible harm, Class III, B.** In OASIS-6, primary PCI with fondaparinux alone caused catheter thrombosis, because it does not inhibit thrombin directly and the contact system in catheters generates thrombin.

**Generally not; limited to the periprocedural period.** Once the artery is stented and the patient is on DAPT, continued anticoagulation adds bleeding without benefit, unless there is another indication (LV thrombus, AF, mechanical valve).
mimic: Fondaparinux in PPCI vs in NSTE-ACS with delayed angiography
Class III in PPCI (catheter thrombosis); Class I in NSTE-ACS when angiography is >24 h away, with a UFH bolus given if PCI follows.
traps: “Fondaparinux is a good anticoagulant for primary PCI”
Class III, B.
decode: Anticoagulant of choice for primary PCI in a patient with HIT? [pattern]
Bivalirudin (I, C).
Which anticoagulant is not recommended in primary PCI? [pattern]
Fondaparinux (III, B).
explain.punch: UFH 70–100 U/kg is the default in primary PCI, enoxaparin and bivalirudin are IIa alternatives (bivalirudin is I in HIT), fondaparinux is harmful, and the anticoagulant stops when the procedure ends.

steps.q:
**For the ESC 2023 ACS antithrombotic algorithm, give:**
a NSTE-ACS anticoagulant: angiography <24 h
b NSTE-ACS anticoagulant: angiography >24 h
c Routine pretreatment: aspirin, P2Y12 before PPCI, P2Y12 in NSTE-ACS
d P2Y12 choice when proceeding to PCI
e Default DAPT, and after 12 months
steps.a:
- **UFH** (I); enoxaparin (IIa)
- **FONDAPARINUX** (I)
- Aspirin **I** • P2Y12 before PPCI **IIb** • routine P2Y12 pretreatment in NSTE-ACS **III**
- **Prasugrel > ticagrelor** (IIa) →
- Aspirin + P2Y12 for **12 months** (I) → **aspirin alone** (I)

explain.intro: Step 6 as one map. Two real questions test it: whether to pre-treat with a P2Y12 inhibitor before angiography, and which anticoagulant to use before angiography in NSTEMI.
why: **NSTE-ACS, angiography <24 hours: UFH (I); enoxaparin (IIa).** UFH is easily reversed and is what the lab will use anyway; enoxaparin is an alternative (IIa, B).

**NSTE-ACS, angiography >24 hours: fondaparinux (I).** In OASIS-5 fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily matched enoxaparin for efficacy at 9 days with about half the major bleeding (about 2.2% vs 4.1%), and lower 30-day mortality, which followed the bleeding difference. If PCI follows, a full UFH bolus is added because of catheter thrombosis (MI-49).

**Aspirin I; P2Y12 before PPCI IIb; routine P2Y12 pretreatment in NSTE-ACS III.** In NSTE-ACS the anatomy is unknown until angiography, and some patients turn out to need CABG (where the P2Y12 blocker adds bleeding) or have no coronary cause. ACCOAST gave prasugrel before angiography and found no fewer ischaemic events but more bleeding; ISAR-REACT 5 used prasugrel without pretreatment in NSTE-ACS and still beat ticagrelor. If angiography is expected after 24 hours, pretreatment may be considered (IIb, C).
**Prasugrel over ticagrelor (IIa) when proceeding to PCI.** ISAR-REACT 5: death, MI or stroke at 1 year 6.9% vs 9.3%, without more bleeding.

**Aspirin + P2Y12 for 12 months (I), then aspirin alone (I).** Shortening is allowed by bleeding risk (ESC: 1-month DAPT in high bleeding risk IIb; 3–6 months IIa). ACC/AHA 2025 add that patients who tolerated ticagrelor-based DAPT can switch to ticagrelor monotherapy from 1 month after PCI (Class 1); see MI-72.
mimic: Fondaparinux: Class I vs Class III
Class I as the anticoagulant in NSTE-ACS with angiography >24 h; Class III as the sole anticoagulant in primary PCI.
traps: “Pre-treatment with a P2Y12 inhibitor is mandatory in NSTEMI”
Routine pretreatment in NSTE-ACS going for early angiography is Class III; withhold until the anatomy is known (ACCOAST, ISAR-REACT 5).
“UFH is superior to enoxaparin” or “enoxaparin is contraindicated for invasive strategy”

Neither is true. DocT keys fondaparinux’s safety advantage over enoxaparin as the only true statement; note that with angiography within 24 hours ESC 2023 prefers UFH, and fondaparinux is the choice when angiography is beyond 24 hours.
decode: NSTEMI for urgent invasive strategy — pre-treat with a P2Y12 inhibitor? [DocT GT]
Generally withhold (especially prasugrel) until the anatomy is known.
Stable NSTEMI awaiting angiography — which anticoagulant statement is true? [DocT GT]
Fondaparinux has less major bleeding than enoxaparin (OASIS-5).
explain.punch: Aspirin for all, P2Y12 at the time of PCI rather than before, prasugrel preferred, UFH if angiography is within 24 hours and fondaparinux if later, then 12 months of DAPT unless bleeding risk shortens it.

steps.q:
**For antiplatelet therapy in the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline, give:**
a The default DAPT duration
b The de-escalation option after PCI, and when
c The preferred P2Y12 inhibitors
d When upstream P2Y12 pretreatment may be considered
steps.a:
- Aspirin + oral P2Y12 for **at least 12 months** - default
- Tolerating DAPT → switch to **TICAGRELOR MONOTHERAPY** **≥1 month** after PCI (to reduce bleeding)
- **Ticagrelor or prasugrel**; clopidogrel if these cannot be used
- NSTE-ACS with angiography **delayed >24 h** - clopidogrel or ticagrelor

explain.intro: Step 4: the antiplatelet rules after PCI. No real question is linked; the testable change is which drug is dropped early, and that ESC and ACC/AHA drop different ones.
why: **Aspirin + oral P2Y12 for at least 12 months — default.** ACC/AHA 2025 gives DAPT for at least 1 year (1, A) in patients not at high bleeding risk, because stent thrombosis and new plaque events cluster in the first year.

**Tolerating DAPT → switch to TICAGRELOR MONOTHERAPY ≥1 month after PCI (to reduce bleeding).** Class 1, A. Once the stent is covered, aspirin adds bleeding more than protection on top of a potent P2Y12 inhibitor; ticagrelor-alone trials (TWILIGHT, ULTIMATE-DAPT) cut bleeding without more ischaemic events. Lesser options are 2b: switching ticagrelor or prasugrel to clopidogrel after 1 month, or single antiplatelet therapy after 1 month if bleeding risk is high.

**Ticagrelor or prasugrel; clopidogrel if these cannot be used.** Class 1 for PCI in STEMI and NSTE-ACS, for fewer MACE and stent thromboses; ACC/AHA names no preference between the two, whereas ESC 2023 prefers prasugrel for patients going to PCI (IIa, B; ISAR-REACT 5). Clopidogrel is for those who cannot take them (prior stroke for prasugrel, oral anticoagulation, high bleeding risk).

**NSTE-ACS with angiography delayed >24 h → clopidogrel or ticagrelor.** It is 2b (‘may be considered’). Routine pretreatment before early angiography is not advised: the anatomy may send the patient to CABG, and prasugrel is not used before the anatomy is known. ESC 2023 also gives pretreatment beyond 24 hours IIb.
mimic: ESC 2023 vs ACC/AHA 2025 at the end of DAPT

ESC: 12 months of DAPT, then usually aspirin alone; single antiplatelet therapy, preferably a P2Y12 inhibitor, after 3–6 months ‘should be considered’ (IIa) if event-free and not high ischaemic risk, and aspirin or P2Y12 monotherapy after 1 month ‘may be considered’ (IIb) only in high bleeding risk; de-escalation in the first 30 days is not recommended. ACC/AHA: can drop aspirin at 1 month and continue ticagrelor alone.
traps: “After 1 month of DAPT, continue aspirin alone” as the ACC/AHA bleeding-reduction option
The Class 1 option keeps ticagrelor and drops aspirin (watch line).
decode: [pattern] ACS, PCI, tolerating ticagrelor-based DAPT, worried about bleeding — ACC/AHA 2025 option at 1 month?
Stop aspirin, continue ticagrelor alone (1, A).
[pattern] NSTE-ACS, angiography planned at 48 h — P2Y12 before the lab?
Clopidogrel or ticagrelor may be considered (2b); not prasugrel.
explain.punch: Default DAPT is 12 months with prasugrel or ticagrelor; ACC/AHA 2025 lets the patient drop aspirin and stay on ticagrelor alone from 1 month, whereas ESC keeps aspirin at the end.

anticoagulant

c Chest pain after sildenafil or tadalafil

**and/or fall** (dynamic change), not a single value.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Antithrombotics, nitrates and troponin
explain.intro: Four separate ACS decisions sit on this card, each tested by a different trap: the anticoagulant when nobody is reperfused, the IV P2Y12 inhibitor, the nitrate ban, and troponin in kidney disease.
why: **Fondaparinux (OASIS-6) — less death/re-MI, no extra major bleeding. Not alone during primary PCI (catheter thrombosis).** Fondaparinux is an indirect factor Xa inhibitor given once daily; in STEMI patients without primary PCI it lowered death or re-infarction without more bleeding. It does not inhibit thrombin at the catheter tip, so if the patient goes to PCI a bolus of UFH is added. ESC 2023 recommends fondaparinux (class I) in NSTE-ACS when early angiography is not planned, advises against it during primary PCI (class III) and gives it IIa alongside streptokinase; it has no separate class for unreperfused STEMI, so the card’s answer rests on OASIS-6.

**Cangrelor — onset seconds, offset ~1 h.** Cangrelor is the only IV P2Y12 inhibitor: reversible, half-life 3–6 minutes, platelet function back within about an hour. Morphine and vomiting delay gut absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors, and IV cangrelor bypasses the gut. It is also the bridge when DAPT must stop for urgent surgery after a recent stent (BRIDGE).
**No nitrates within 24 h (sildenafil) / 48 h (tadalafil) — profound hypotension.** Both nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors raise cGMP in vascular smooth muscle; together they cause severe vasodilation.

**Chronically raised; diagnose MI by a rise and/or fall (dynamic change), not a single value.** Chronic kidney disease and chronic myocardial injury raise baseline troponin; the Fourth Universal Definition requires a rise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th percentile, plus clinical evidence of ischaemia.
mimic: Cangrelor vs GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors
Cangrelor blocks P2Y12, reversible, offset about an hour. Eptifibatide and tirofiban block GP IIb/IIIa; abciximab binds platelets for days.
traps: “Enoxaparin or UFH” as the best anticoagulant when no reperfusion is given
Fondaparinux (23% right).
“Tirofiban or eptifibatide” as IV P2Y12 bridging
Cangrelor (35% right on the mini test; 80% in GT2).
“A single troponin above the 99th percentile in CKD 4 = MI”
A dynamic rise and/or fall is needed (GT3 lost).
decode: Recent stent, on DAPT, septic shock needing urgent surgery — IV antiplatelet bridge? [DocT GT, 80%]
Cangrelor infusion.
explain.punch: No reperfusion: fondaparinux; IV P2Y12: cangrelor (also the surgical bridge); no nitrates within 24 h of sildenafil or 48 h of tadalafil; in CKD diagnose MI by a troponin rise and/or fall.

questions.text: NSTE-ACS, risk scores and the invasive path

steps.q:
**Sort NSTE-ACS by risk and give the invasive strategy for each:**
a Very high-risk features (six)
b High-risk features (four)
c Strategy for very high risk
d Strategy for high risk
e Strategy for non-high risk
steps.a:
**Very high risk** | **High risk**
- Haemodynamic instability / cardiogenic shock | - Confirmed NSTEMI (ESC algorithms)
- Recurrent / refractory chest pain | - GRACE >140
- Acute HF from ongoing ischaemia | - Transient ST elevation
- Life-threatening arrhythmia / arrest after presentation | - Dynamic ST / T changes
- Mechanical complications |
- Recurrent dynamic ECG changes |
- Very high → **IMMEDIATE** transfer and invasive strategy (<2 h)
- High → **early (<24 h)** invasive strategy - **IIa**
- Non-high → **selective** / inpatient invasive strategy - I

explain.intro: Step 4 changes the question: without ST elevation the artery is usually not fully closed, so the decision is how fast to do angiography, and risk sets the speed. No real question is linked; the class change in ESC 2023 is the likely target.
why: **Very high risk: haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock, recurrent or refractory chest pain, acute HF from ongoing ischaemia, life-threatening arrhythmia or arrest after presentation, mechanical complications, recurrent dynamic ECG changes.** Each means myocardium is dying now or the patient may not survive the wait, so these behave like a STEMI.
**High risk: confirmed NSTEMI (ESC algorithms), GRACE >140, transient ST elevation, dynamic ST/T changes.** A rising troponin or a changing ECG marks an active thrombus.
**Very high risk: immediate transfer and invasive strategy (<2 hours).** Class I, C.

**High risk: early (<24 hours) invasive strategy, IIa.** ESC 2023 downgraded this from I (2020) to IIa, A, because trials of early versus delayed angiography showed no mortality benefit overall (benefit only in subgroups such as GRACE >140).

**Non-high risk: selective or inpatient invasive strategy, Class I.** The Class I recommendation is to do angiography during the admission (or selectively after non-invasive testing), not within 24 hours. ACC/AHA 2025 similarly recommend an invasive approach during the admission for intermediate- and high-risk patients.
mimic: Very high-risk NSTE-ACS vs STEMI
Both go to the lab within 2 hours; but lysis is never used in NSTE-ACS, because the artery is not occluded and lysis adds bleeding without benefit.
traps: “Early invasive strategy within 24 hours is Class I in high-risk NSTE-ACS”
It is IIa in ESC 2023; the Class I is for an invasive strategy during the admission.
decode: NSTEMI with refractory pain and hypotension despite treatment — timing of angiography? [pattern]
Immediate, within 2 hours.
Stable NSTEMI with rising troponin, GRACE 150 — timing? [pattern]
Early, within 24 hours (IIa).
explain.punch: In NSTE-ACS, risk sets the clock: very high risk under 2 hours (I), high risk under 24 hours (only IIa now), everyone else during the admission or selectively.

steps.q:
**For the GRACE score, give:**
a The nine variables
b What the nomogram predicts
c The cut-off used in ESC algorithms
steps.a:
**Background** | **Admission / stay**
- Age | - Heart rate
- History of heart failure | - Systolic BP
- History of AMI | - ST depression
| - Serum creatinine
| - Elevated cardiac enzymes
| - No in-hospital PCI
- **6-month mortality** after ACS
- **GRACE >140** = high risk (early invasive, MI-43; discharge threshold, MI-32)

explain.intro: Step 6 starts with grading the risk. No real question is linked; GRACE is tested through its cut-off of 140 and through the contrast with TIMI (MI-69).
why: **Background: age, history of heart failure, history of AMI. Admission / stay: heart rate, systolic BP, ST depression, serum creatinine, elevated cardiac enzymes, no in-hospital PCI.** These are the nine variables of the post-discharge (6-month) nomogram. The original in-hospital GRACE model uses eight: age, heart rate, systolic BP, creatinine, Killip class, cardiac arrest at admission, ST deviation and raised enzymes. Each variable is weighted, so age and haemodynamics count far more than any single item.
**6-month mortality after ACS.** The current calculator (GRACE 2.0) also gives in-hospital and 1-year figures.

**GRACE >140 = high risk (early invasive, MI-43; discharge threshold, MI-32).** In NSTE-ACS, GRACE >140 is one of the high-risk features that call for angiography within 24 hours; below 140, with a negative rule-out and no pain, early discharge is acceptable.
mimic: GRACE vs Killip
Killip is a bedside HF class (one of GRACE’s in-hospital inputs); GRACE combines many variables into a mortality estimate.
traps: “GRACE predicts 14-day events”
That is TIMI; GRACE predicts death, here at 6 months.
decode: NSTEMI, GRACE 160, stable — timing of angiography? [pattern]
Early invasive, within 24 hours.
explain.punch: GRACE weights nine variables into the risk of death at 6 months; above 140 the patient is high risk and goes for angiography within 24 hours.

steps.q:
**For the TIMI UA / NSTEMI score, give:**
a The seven one-point variables
b The outcome it predicts, and when
c Event rates at 0-1 and 6-7 points
steps.a:
**1 point each** |
- Age ≥65 | - ≥2 rest-angina episodes in 24 h
- ≥3 CAD risk factors | - ST deviation
- Known CAD (stenosis ≥50%) | - Elevated cardiac markers
- Aspirin in last 7 days |
- Death, new / recurrent MI, or urgent revascularisation **through 14 days**
- **0-1** → **4.7%** • 2 → 8.3% • 3 → 13.2% • 4 → 19.9% • 5 → 26.2% • **6-7** → **40.9%**

explain.intro: Step 6 with the simpler tool. No real question is linked; the test is usually the variables, especially aspirin use, which surprises people.
why: **Age ≥65, ≥3 CAD risk factors, known CAD (stenosis ≥50%), aspirin in the last 7 days, ≥2 rest-angina episodes in 24 h, ST deviation, elevated cardiac markers.** Aspirin use counts because an ACS that breaks through aspirin marks a more aggressive, more thrombotic disease.
**Death, new / recurrent MI, or urgent revascularisation through 14 days.** A short-term composite, not mortality at 6 months.

**0–1 → 4.7%; 2 → 8.3%; 3 → 13.2%; 4 → 19.9%; 5 → 26.2%; 6–7 → 40.9%.** The risk climbs steeply with each point, which is why higher scores were linked to greater benefit from enoxaparin and an early invasive approach.
mimic: TIMI UA/NSTEMI score vs TIMI STEMI score
The STEMI score is a different, weighted tool for 30-day mortality; the seven one-point items are the UA/NSTEMI score.
traps: “Aspirin use lowers the TIMI score”
It adds a point.
decode: Which is a TIMI UA/NSTEMI variable — aspirin in the last 7 days, heart rate, creatinine? [pattern]
Aspirin in the last 7 days.
explain.punch: TIMI gives one point for each of seven items, aspirin use included, and predicts death, MI or urgent revascularisation at 14 days, from 4.7% at 0–1 points to 40.9% at 6–7.

steps.q:
**For radial vs femoral access, give:**
a What radial access lowers
b The trial behind the transfusion benefit
c The trials behind the cost and mortality benefit
d When femoral is used
steps.a:
- **Bleeding**, **vascular complications** (pseudoaneurysm), need for **transfusion**; better overall survival
- **MATRIX**
- **RIVAL** and **RIFLE-STEACS**
- Only when radial is **not feasible** - higher complication risk

explain.intro: Still in step 5: where the catheter goes in. No real question is linked, but the femoral bleeding questions on MI-46 are the other side of this card.
why: **Bleeding, vascular complications (pseudoaneurysm), need for transfusion; better overall survival.** The radial artery is superficial and compressible over bone, and a bleed there cannot track into the retroperitoneum; in ACS patients loaded with antithrombotics, access-site bleeding is the main avoidable bleed, and bleeding itself raises mortality. ESC 2023: radial access is the standard, Class I, A.
**MATRIX.** MATRIX (about 8,400 ACS patients) found fewer major bleeds and transfusions with radial access, and also lower all-cause mortality.

**RIVAL and RIFLE-STEACS.** RIVAL’s overall primary outcome was neutral, with fewer vascular complications and a benefit in the STEMI subgroup; RIFLE-STEACS (STEMI) found lower cardiac mortality (about 5% vs 9%), less bleeding and a shorter hospital stay, which is the cost benefit.
**Only when radial is not feasible; higher complication risk.** Examples are a poor radial pulse, need for large-bore devices or mechanical support, or a failed radial attempt.
mimic: Radial complication vs femoral complication
Radial: artery occlusion, spasm, small haematoma. Femoral: retroperitoneal bleed, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula.
traps: “Radial access only reduces bleeding, not death”
MATRIX and RIFLE-STEACS both showed lower mortality.
decode: Preferred access for PCI in ACS, and the trial behind it? [pattern]
Radial (I, A); MATRIX.
explain.punch: Radial access is the standard because ACS patients are fully anticoagulated and a compressible artery cannot bleed into the retroperitoneum; femoral is for when radial cannot be done.

steps.q:
**Sort the complications of PCI:**
a Local
b Coronary
c Contrast-related
d Others
steps.a:
**Group** | **Complications**
**Local** | Bleeding, haematoma, infection, pseudoaneurysm, compartment syndrome
**Coronary** | Dissection, embolism, spasm
**Contrast** | Contrast nephropathy, allergic reaction, CHF
**Others** | Access-vessel dissection, stroke, death
bank_lines: Marrow: Retroperitoneal haematoma after PCI follows a femoral puncture ABOVE the inguinal ligament: back/flank pain and hypotension with little groin swelling — diagnose by non-contrast CT; radial access avoids it.

DocT GT: Hypotension hours after an uncomplicated RADIAL PCI with no new ECG change → urgent bedside echo for tamponade from coronary or wire perforation (or a new mechanical complication); retroperitoneal bleeding belongs to femoral access, stent thrombosis to new ST elevation.

explain.intro: Step 5 ends with what goes wrong after PCI. The one real question is the retroperitoneal bleed, and the card layer adds how to tell it from tamponade and stent thrombosis.
why: **Local: bleeding, haematoma, infection, pseudoaneurysm, compartment syndrome.** A femoral puncture above the inguinal ligament cannot be compressed against the femoral head, so blood tracks into the retroperitoneum: back or flank pain and hypotension with little groin swelling. Diagnose with non-contrast CT; radial access avoids it.
**Coronary: dissection, embolism, spasm.** A wire or balloon can dissect or perforate the coronary; a perforation fills the pericardium and causes tamponade, sometimes hours later.
**Contrast: contrast nephropathy, allergic reaction, CHF.** Contrast is a volume and osmotic load (heart failure) and damages the renal medulla; hydration and limiting volume are the prevention.
**Others: access-vessel dissection, stroke, death.** Catheters crossing the aortic arch can dislodge atheroma or thrombus to the brain.
mimic: Retroperitoneal haematoma vs groin haematoma
A groin haematoma is visible and compressible; a retroperitoneal bleed shows only as pain and shock.
traps: “Retroperitoneal bleed” after a radial PCI
It belongs to femoral access; after a radial case think tamponade.
decode: 2 h after femoral catheterisation: hypotension and back pain — diagnosis? [Marrow]
Retroperitoneal bleeding.
Hypotension hours after an uncomplicated radial PCI, ECG unchanged — first test? [pattern]
Bedside echo for tamponade.
explain.punch: Shock after PCI has three main answers: retroperitoneal bleed if femoral, tamponade if a coronary was perforated, stent thrombosis if the ST segments rise again.

steps.q:
**For CABG in ACS, give:**
a The three indications
b The problem with early CABG
c The optimal timing
d When CABG is done emergently
e Antiplatelet management afterwards
steps.a:
- Anatomy **unsuitable for PCI** • **failed PCI** • **mechanical complications** (coronary dissection, VSD, papillary muscle rupture)
- **Higher mortality** (non-randomised data)
- After **3-7 days**
- **Refractory ischaemia**, **cardiogenic shock**
- A **second antiplatelet** is typically given after the procedure
bank_lines: DocT GT: Before URGENT CABG stop clopidogrel or ticagrelor ≥24 h (ACC/AHA class I) to cut bleeding; for elective CABG ≥3 days ticagrelor, ≥5 days clopidogrel, ≥7 days prasugrel. Aspirin is continued; the irreversible/long-acting P2Y12 blocker is the drug to stop first.

DocT GT: The short-acting GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors eptifibatide and tirofiban (reversible, renally cleared) need stopping only 2–4 h before urgent CABG because platelet function recovers within hours; abciximab binds irreversibly and needs ≥12 h.

explain.intro: The deck ends with surgery, where the antiplatelet drugs become the problem. Both real questions ask how long before urgent CABG each drug must be stopped.
why: **Anatomy unsuitable for PCI, failed PCI, mechanical complications (coronary dissection, VSD, papillary muscle rupture).** Left main or complex multivessel disease is the commonest anatomical reason.
**Higher mortality (non-randomised data).** Operating in the first days means bypass on freshly infarcted, reperfusion-injured myocardium, in a patient loaded with antiplatelets.
**After 3–7 days.** For a stable patient, waiting lets the infarct settle and the P2Y12 blocker wear off.
**Refractory ischaemia, cardiogenic shock.** ESC: emergency CABG for ACS-related shock when PCI of the infarct artery is not feasible or has failed (I, B).
**A second antiplatelet is typically given after the procedure.** ESC 2023: resume DAPT after CABG for at least 12 months (I, C), because the ACS risk is still there.
mimic: Short-acting GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors vs oral P2Y12 blockers before surgery
Eptifibatide and tirofiban are reversible and renally cleared, so platelets recover within hours; oral P2Y12 blockers need a day to a week.
traps: “Continue ticagrelor until surgery” or “stop 2–4 hours before”
Stop at least 24 hours before urgent on-pump CABG.
“Stop eptifibatide 24 hours before”
Only 2–4 hours are needed.
decode: NSTEMI on aspirin + ticagrelor, left main disease, urgent CABG — ticagrelor? [DocT GT]
Stop 24 hours before.
STEMI on eptifibatide, urgent CABG — minimum stop time? [DocT GT]
2–4 hours.
explain.punch: CABG in ACS is for anatomy PCI cannot fix, failed PCI, mechanical complications or shock. Before urgent surgery keep aspirin, stop clopidogrel or ticagrelor 24 hours and eptifibatide or tirofiban 2–4 hours, and restart DAPT afterwards.

steps.q:
**For the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline, give the position on:**
a Complete revascularisation in STEMI and NSTE-ACS
b Intravascular imaging (IVUS / OCT)
c Access site
d Microaxial flow pump in AMI shock
e Routine IABP or VA-ECMO in shock
f Where shock patients should be treated
steps.a:
- **Recommended (I)** - index or staged; not in cardiogenic shock (culprit-only, CS-36)
- **Class 1** to guide PCI
- **Radial** preferred
- **Reasonable (IIa)** in selected patients - DANGER-SHOCK (MI-63)
- **Not recommended (III)**
- Transfer to **shock centres** (Class 1)

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Revascularisation, imaging, access and shock (ACC/AHA 2025)
explain.intro: Step 5 is what is done to the arteries. No real question is linked; the testable point is that complete revascularisation reverses in shock, and that devices help only in a narrow group.
why: **Recommended (I), index or staged; not in cardiogenic shock (culprit-only, CS-36).** Non-culprit lesions in a stable patient cause later MI, so treating them cuts MACE (COMPLETE): Class 1 in selected stable STEMI and in NSTE-ACS without left main disease or a plan for CABG. In shock routine non-culprit PCI at the index procedure is 3: Harm in both, because the extra contrast and time raised death or renal replacement in CULPRIT-SHOCK.

**Class 1 to guide PCI.** 1, A for stenting the left main or complex lesions: IVUS or OCT shows stent under-expansion and malapposition that angiography misses, the causes of stent thrombosis and restenosis.

**Radial preferred.** 1, A: fewer bleeds, fewer vascular complications and lower death than femoral, because the radial artery is superficial and compressible (the femoral retroperitoneal bleed is the Top-up).

**Reasonable (IIa) in selected patients — DANGER-SHOCK (MI-63).** 2a, B-R in STEMI with severe or refractory LV-dominant shock: DanGer Shock cut 180-day death (45.8% vs 58.5%) but with more bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal failure, and it excluded comatose cardiac-arrest survivors and RV shock.
**Not recommended (III).** Routine IABP or VA-ECMO is 3: No benefit (IABP-SHOCK II, ECLS-SHOCK: no survival gain). VA-ECMO raises afterload on a failing LV; it is a rescue tool, not routine.

**Transfer to shock centres (Class 1).** Shock outcomes are better where the team, round-the-clock PCI, mechanical support and cardiac surgery are all available, so the sickest patients are moved to such a hub early. Some guideline summaries (Cleveland Clinic) report this as a Class 1 recommendation, but the classed shock statements in the ACC/AHA 2025 text are about revascularisation and devices; the hub-and-spoke model with early transfer of refractory shock to a Level 1 shock centre comes from the ACC 2025 concise clinical guidance on cardiogenic shock, which carries no class (see FLAGS). The exam answer is still a centre with shock expertise.
mimic: Stable multivessel ACS vs multivessel ACS in shock
Stable: treat all significant lesions, at the index procedure or staged. Shock: culprit only at the index procedure.
ACC/AHA 2025 vs ESC 2023 classes

ESC 2023: complete revascularisation is recommended (I) in stable STEMI, at the index PCI or within 45 days, but only ‘should be considered’ (IIa) in NSTE-ACS; intravascular imaging ‘should be considered’ (IIa). ACC/AHA 2025 makes both Class 1.
traps: “Complete revascularisation at the index procedure in cardiogenic shock”
3: Harm (CULPRIT-SHOCK); the notes’ shock table is outdated here (watch line).
“Impella for every AMI shock”
Only selected STEMI LV shock (DanGer criteria), at the price of more complications.
decode: [pattern] STEMI in shock, three-vessel disease — what to stent at the index procedure?
The culprit only.
[pattern] AMI shock — routine IABP?
No (3: No benefit, IABP-SHOCK II).
explain.punch: Treat all significant lesions in the stable patient but only the culprit in shock, image complex lesions, go radial, and reserve a microaxial pump for selected STEMI shock; routine IABP and VA-ECMO bring no survival benefit.

questions.text: When the infarct is complicated: rhythm, failure and shock

steps.q:
**For ventricular arrhythmias after MI, give:**
a The reperfusion arrhythmia, its cause and treatment
b VT - management if unstable
c VT - management if stable
d NSVT - management
steps.a:
- **Accelerated idioventricular rhythm** - reperfusion + enhanced automaticity of ventricular pacemaker cells; **BENIGN**, usually no treatment
- **Immediate cardioversion** + correct **K+ and Mg2+**
- Correct electrolytes; **beta-blocker or amiodarone**
- Correct electrolytes; **beta-blocker**
bank_lines: DocT GT: Ventricular arrhythmias 24–72 h after a large MI (PVCs, NSVT, VT) arise mainly from ABNORMAL AUTOMATICITY in partially depolarised ischaemic myocytes and Purkinje fibres, driven by catecholamines and low K/Mg; AIVR at reperfusion is enhanced normal automaticity; LATE sustained monomorphic VT (weeks–years) is scar re-entry. Afterdepolarisations belong to long QT (early) and digoxin/Ca overload (delayed).

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Ventricular arrhythmias after MI
explain.intro: Step 2 sorts ventricular arrhythmias by when they appear, because timing tells you the mechanism and the treatment. All four real questions ask the mechanism of VT at 48 hours, which the card does not state: the answer is abnormal automaticity.
why: **Accelerated idioventricular rhythm — reperfusion + enhanced automaticity of ventricular pacemaker cells; BENIGN, usually no treatment.** Washout of the opened artery speeds normal Purkinje pacemakers until they outrun the sinus node: a regular wide-complex rhythm only a little faster than sinus, which gives way when the sinus rate rises. It is a marker that reperfusion worked; suppressing it with an antiarrhythmic can leave no rhythm at all.

**VT unstable: immediate cardioversion + correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺.** Pulseless VT is treated as VF on the arrest algorithm. Potassium is kept at 4 mmol/L or above and magnesium in the high-normal range, because low levels lower the threshold for every mechanism.

**VT stable: correct electrolytes; beta-blocker or amiodarone.** Catecholamines drive early post-MI VT, so a beta-blocker treats the cause; amiodarone suppresses recurrence. Recurrent VT means ongoing ischaemia until angiography proves otherwise (MI-59).
**NSVT: correct electrolytes; beta-blocker.** Runs of NSVT in the first 48 hours are common and do not predict late sudden death; they need no antiarrhythmic and no ICD decision.
mimic: AIVR vs slow VT
AIVR runs near the sinus rate, starts and stops with sinus slowing and is harmless; VT is faster and sustained.
Enhanced normal vs abnormal automaticity
Normal automaticity is a pacemaker cell firing faster (AIVR); abnormal automaticity is a working myocyte, partly depolarised by ischaemia, that starts firing on its own (VT at 24–72 h).
traps: “Re-entry” for VT 48 hours after MI

61–67% got the NSVT version right. Re-entry is the mechanism of very early VF and of late scar VT; at 24–72 hours abnormal automaticity is the best answer. Re-entry is still the main mechanism of sustained post-MI VT overall, so choose it only when the stem is weeks to years after MI.
“Enhanced normal automaticity” for VT at 48 hours
That is AIVR at reperfusion; VT at 48 hours comes from non-pacemaker cells, which is abnormal automaticity.
“Early or delayed afterdepolarisations”
EADs belong to long QT and torsades; DADs to digoxin and calcium overload. Neither is the post-MI answer.
Treating AIVR with amiodarone or lidocaine
It is benign and a sign of reperfusion; suppressing it can unmask asystole.
decode: VT 48 hours after a large anterior MI — mechanism? [DocT GT ×2]
Abnormal automaticity (83–87% right).
Stable NSVT 48 hours after MI — mechanism? [DocT GT ×2]
Abnormal automaticity, not re-entry (61–67% right).
Wide regular rhythm at 80/min just after the artery is opened — action? [pattern]
AIVR: none.
explain.punch: Read the clock: VF in the first hours is ischaemic re-entry, AIVR at reperfusion is harmless enhanced automaticity, VT at 24–72 hours is abnormal automaticity, and VT weeks later is scar re-entry. Early arrhythmias need electrolytes, a beta-blocker and an open artery, not prophylactic drugs.
