steps.q:
**For AV block after MI, give:**
a Proximal block - types, artery, course, pacing
b Distal block - type, artery, course, pacing
c Bradycardia / high-grade block with haemodynamic intolerance - the three steps (ESC)
steps.a:
| **Proximal** | **Distal**
**Type** | 1st degree, **Mobitz I** | **3rd degree**
**Artery** | **RCA** (inferior MI) | **LAD** (anterior MI)
**Course** | Usually **transient**, resolves with reperfusion | Life-threatening
**Pacemaker** | Not typically needed | Often **required**
- **IV positive chronotropes** (epinephrine, vasopressin and/or atropine) - I, C
- **Temporary pacing** if they fail - I, C
- **Urgent angiography** if no prior reperfusion - I, C
Bradycardia drugs and doses: ACLS-35 to ACLS-40.
bank_lines: DocT GT: AV block complicates 10–25% of acute MIs and is usually transient, mostly first-degree or Mobitz I. Inferior MI gives AV-nodal block with a narrow escape that usually resolves; anterior MI gives infranodal block with a wide escape that needs pacing.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → AV block after MI
explain.intro: Step 3: the level of the block follows the artery. Both real questions are about the inferior–anterior split; one has a wrong key and the other has two true options.
why: **Proximal block: 1st degree, Mobitz I; RCA (inferior MI); usually transient, resolves with reperfusion; pacemaker not typically needed.** The RCA supplies the AV node in most people, and inferior MI adds vagal (Bezold–Jarisch) tone and adenosine release at the node. Nodal block has a narrow junctional escape at 40–60/min that keeps the patient perfused, responds to atropine and usually recovers within days. Inferior MI can also cause complete heart block at the node; it behaves the same way and still usually resolves.

**Distal block: 3rd degree; LAD (anterior MI); life-threatening; pacemaker often required.** Septal branches of the LAD supply the His bundle and bundle branches, so block here means a large septal infarct. Mobitz II or new bifascicular block warns of it; the escape is wide and slow (under 40/min) and unreliable. Atropine works on the node only and may worsen infranodal block by speeding the atrial rate.

**Bradycardia / high-grade block with haemodynamic intolerance: IV positive chronotropes (epinephrine, vasopressin and/or atropine) — I, C; temporary pacing if they fail — I, C; urgent angiography if no prior reperfusion — I, C.** Drugs buy minutes, the pacing wire gives a dependable rate, and reopening the artery treats the cause. AHA 2025 ACLS doses: atropine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes to 3 mg, then epinephrine infusion or pacing. ESC 2023 adds that a permanent pacemaker is recommended only if high-degree block persists at least 5 days after MI (I, C), and pacing is not recommended once the block has resolved (III, B), because most post-MI block recovers.
mimic: Mobitz I vs Mobitz II after MI
Mobitz I (progressive PR lengthening) is nodal, inferior and benign; Mobitz II (fixed PR, sudden dropped beat) is infranodal, anterior and needs pacing.
Narrow vs wide escape in complete block
Narrow escape at 40–60/min means a junctional pacemaker above the block (inferior); wide at under 40/min means a ventricular pacemaker below it (anterior).
traps: DocT GT keys “Mobitz I, benign, resolves with atropine” for block after an ANTERIOR MI
The key contradicts its own explanation. Block after anterior MI is infranodal (LAD, His–Purkinje), does not respond to atropine and needs pacing: choose the His–Purkinje/transvenous pacing option.
“Anterior MI most commonly produces 2nd and 3rd degree block”
Only 15% got this question right. Inferior MI causes more AV block of every degree, including complete block; anterior block is rarer but far more dangerous.
Two true options: “AV block transiently develops in 10–25%” and “inferior MI most commonly produces 1st and 2nd degree block”
Both are true; the key is the transient-block statement, so pick it when both appear.
“Anterior MI gives a narrow-complex escape”
Anterior block is below the His bundle, so the escape is wide.
decode: Anterior MI with this ECG (block) — level and management? [DocT GT]
His–Purkinje; transvenous pacing (key says Mobitz I/atropine, which is wrong).
True statement about AV block in acute MI? [DocT GT]
Transient AV block occurs in 10–25% (keyed); the inferior-MI statement is also true.
Inferior MI, complete heart block, narrow escape at 50/min, BP 70 — sequence? [pattern]
Atropine/epinephrine, then temporary pacing; reperfuse if not already done.
explain.punch: Inferior MI blocks the AV node: narrow escape, atropine works, it recovers. Anterior MI blocks the His–Purkinje system: wide escape, atropine fails, pace. If haemodynamics fail, chronotropes then a pacing wire then the cath lab, all Class I.

steps.q:
**For acute heart failure complicating ACS, give:**
a The standard therapy
b Haemodynamic support - the two drug classes and examples
c The prognostic consequences
d The two clinical syndromes
steps.a:
- **Diuretics**, **vasodilators**, **NIV**
- **Vasopressor** for hypotension (norepinephrine); **inotrope** for output (dobutamine)
- Longer stay, more **mechanical ventilation**, more **RRT**
- **Pulmonary congestion**; **cardiogenic shock / low output / hypotension**
bank_lines: Marrow: Killip class: I no heart failure; II S3 and/or rales in <50% of lung fields; III frank pulmonary oedema (rales >50%); IV cardiogenic shock — mortality rises steeply with each class.

DocT GT: Hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema (SCAPE): high-dose IV nitroglycerin (titratable preload and afterload reduction) plus NIV/CPAP first; most patients are redistributed, not overloaded, so 'loop diuretic and wait' is too slow. Hydralazine is unpredictable with reflex tachycardia, labetalol's β-blockade depresses a failing LV, oral ACEi is too slow; intubate only for NIV failure or falling GCS.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Acute heart failure in ACS
explain.intro: Step 4 starts with the pump. Lost myocardium gives either congestion with a blood pressure, or low output with hypotension; the three real questions test the first-line move in each.
why: **Diuretics, vasodilators, NIV.** In pulmonary oedema with a good or high blood pressure the problem is often redistribution into the lungs under high afterload, not excess total water. IV nitroglycerin reduces preload at low dose and afterload at high dose, works in minutes and is titratable; CPAP/NIV recruits flooded alveoli and lowers LV afterload. Loop diuretics help the overloaded but act more slowly.

**Vasopressor for hypotension (norepinephrine); inotrope for output (dobutamine).** Norepinephrine raises perfusion pressure with less tachycardia and arrhythmia than dopamine (SOAP II, worse in the cardiogenic subgroup) and less refractory shock than epinephrine after MI (OptimaCC). Dobutamine is added when output stays low once pressure is restored. ESC grades both only IIb, because no inotrope or pressor has been shown to improve survival.

**Longer stay, more mechanical ventilation, more RRT.** ESC 2023 links acute HF in ACS with renal failure, respiratory failure, pneumonia and death; Killip class rises with each step (I no HF; II S3 or rales <50% of the fields; III frank pulmonary oedema; IV shock), and so does mortality.

**Pulmonary congestion; cardiogenic shock / low output / hypotension.** The first is ‘wet and warm’, the second ‘wet and cold’. Both need emergency echo and angiography (ESC 2023), because a mechanical complication or an occluded artery may be the cause.
mimic: Hypertensive pulmonary oedema (SCAPE) vs cardiogenic shock
High BP: nitrates and NIV, avoid pressors. Low BP and cold periphery: norepinephrine, then inotrope, revascularise; nitrates are contraindicated.
traps: “Loop diuretic and wait” in BP 180/100 pulmonary oedema
Too slow and aims at the wrong problem; 65% chose nitrates with NIV.
“Intubate now” in an alert patient with SpO₂ 88%
Try NIV first; intubate for NIV failure, exhaustion or a falling GCS.
IV hydralazine or labetalol for hypertensive pulmonary oedema
Hydralazine is unpredictable and causes reflex tachycardia; labetalol’s beta-blockade depresses a failing LV (94% chose nitroglycerin).
“Dopamine” as the first vasopressor in post-MI shock
76% chose norepinephrine. Dopamine causes more arrhythmia and was associated with higher mortality in cardiogenic shock.
decode: Pink frothy sputum, BP 180/100, SpO₂ 88%, alert — next step? [DocT GT]
Nitrates and NIV.
Hypertensive pulmonary oedema, BP 210/120 — initial drug? [DocT GT]
IV nitroglycerin.
Post-MI cardiogenic shock — first-line vasopressor? [DocT GT]
Norepinephrine.
explain.punch: Congestion with a pressure gets nitrates and NIV (diuretic if overloaded); low output and hypotension gets norepinephrine first and dobutamine for output, then the artery opened. Each Killip class up raises mortality.

parts.q: Killip class III vs IV? [Marrow line]
parts.a: III is frank pulmonary oedema (rales over more than half the lung fields); IV is cardiogenic shock.

steps.q:
**For cardiogenic shock in STEMI, give the class of:**
a Immediate PCI (or CABG)
b Arterial line, immediate echo, early repair of mechanical complications
c Fibrinolysis when PCI is unavailable within 120 min
d IABP for mechanical complications
e PA catheter, ultrafiltration, inotropes / vasopressors, short-term MCS
f Routine IABP
steps.a:
**Recommendation** | **Class**
**Immediate PCI**; emergency CABG if unsuitable / PCI fails | I, B
Arterial line • immediate Doppler echo • early heart-team repair of mechanical complications • O2 / ventilation by gases | I, C
Fibrinolysis if PPCI not possible <120 min (mechanical cause excluded) | IIa, C
IABP - shock from **mechanical complications** | IIa, C
PA catheter (IIb, B) • ultrafiltration (IIb, B) • inotropes / vasopressors (IIb, C) • short-term MCS (IIb, C) | IIb
**Routine IABP** | **III, B**
bank_lines: Marrow: AMI cardiogenic-shock risk: older age, anterior MI, multivessel disease, prior MI, diabetes, prior HF (a first posterior infarct with shock → look for a mechanical complication or RV involvement). Lactate >2 mmol/L (the higher the worse) and admission glucose independently predict death; transaminases rise from hypoperfusion; cystatin C/NGAL add little over creatinine.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Cardiogenic shock in STEMI (ESC)
explain.intro: Step 4 in classes. All three real questions ask the one thing that saves life in post-MI shock: opening the artery, by PCI even when the patient looks too sick.
why: **Immediate PCI; emergency CABG if unsuitable / PCI fails: I, B.** Shock is a large ischaemic territory failing; only reperfusion stops it. In the SHOCK trial early revascularisation did not reach significance at 30 days but saved about 13 lives per 100 at 6 months. CULPRIT-SHOCK then showed that PCI of the culprit artery only, with any other lesions staged later, beat immediate multivessel PCI (ESC 2023: culprit-only at the index procedure, Class I).

**Arterial line, immediate Doppler echo, early heart-team repair of mechanical complications, O₂ / ventilation by gases: I, C.** The echo separates LV failure from RV infarction, tamponade, VSR and acute MR, each of which changes treatment.
**Fibrinolysis if PPCI not possible <120 min (mechanical cause excluded): IIa, C.** Lysis works poorly at low perfusion pressure, but is better than no reperfusion when the lab is far.

**IABP for shock from mechanical complications: IIa, C.** Deflating just before systole lowers afterload, which reduces the regurgitant or shunt fraction and improves forward flow while awaiting surgery.

**PA catheter (IIb, B), ultrafiltration (IIb, B), inotropes / vasopressors (IIb, C), short-term MCS (IIb, C).** Each can be used but none has shown a survival benefit; ESC 2023 keeps short-term MCS at IIb, C, while ACC/AHA 2025 makes a microaxial flow pump IIa in selected STEMI shock (MI-63).
**Routine IABP: III, B.** IABP-SHOCK II (n 600) found no mortality benefit at 30 days, 1 year or 6 years.
mimic: Shock from LV pump failure vs from a mechanical complication
Pump failure: PCI ± MCS, no routine IABP. Mechanical complication (new murmur, tamponade): IABP is IIa as a bridge to surgery.
Inferior STEMI shock with clear lungs
Think RV infarction: fluids, avoid nitrates, reperfuse.
traps: “Immediate fibrinolysis” when PCI is available in 75 minutes
Within 120 minutes primary PCI wins, and in shock even more so.
“Routine IABP” in STEMI shock
Class III since IABP-SHOCK II; only for mechanical complications.
“Multivessel PCI at the index procedure” in shock (the notes call it IIa)
CULPRIT-SHOCK: culprit-only first; stage the rest.
decode: STEMI with cardiogenic shock, door-to-balloon 75 min — reperfusion strategy? [DocT GT]
Primary PCI.
Treatment of choice: STEMI with cardiogenic shock? [Marrow]
Revascularisation with PCI (I, B); routine IABP III.
Inferior STEMI with shock — next step? [Marrow]
Primary PCI.
explain.punch: In STEMI shock open the culprit artery now (PCI, or CABG if not feasible), echo immediately and fix any mechanical lesion; routine IABP is Class III, and drugs, PA catheters and MCS are only IIb.

parts.q: Who gets shock after MI, and what predicts death? [Marrow line]
parts.a: Older age, anterior MI, multivessel disease, prior MI, diabetes, prior HF; a first posterior or inferior infarct with shock suggests a mechanical complication or RV infarction. Lactate >2 mmol/L and admission glucose independently predict death.

shock.

b Vasoactive drug if SBP is 96
c If SBP is below 90

steps.a:
**Shock + STEMI** → **transfer for**
**revascularisation regardless of delay**
a **Immediate transfer** for PCI/CABG, whatever
the delay. Culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK).
b **Dobutamine** — low output without frank

bank_lines: DocT GT: Levosimendan also keeps working under β-blockade: it sensitises troponin C to calcium (and opens K-ATP channels), bypassing the β-receptor/cAMP pathway, so ESC prefers it (or milrinone) over dobutamine in β-blocked patients. Dopamine, adrenaline and dopexamine all act through β-receptors and lose effect.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → STEMI with cardiogenic shock
explain.intro: Shock changes the reperfusion rule of CAR-17: lysis needs a perfusion pressure to reach the clot, so the priority becomes mechanical revascularisation. The card then chooses the vasoactive drug by the blood pressure and by any β-blockade.
why: **Immediate transfer for PCI/CABG, whatever the delay. Culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK).** In the SHOCK trial early revascularisation improved long-term survival; lytics work poorly at low perfusion pressure. CULPRIT-SHOCK found culprit-only PCI better than immediate multivessel PCI (death or renal replacement at 30 days 45.9% vs 55.4%). ESC 2023 adds that fibrinolysis should be considered (IIa) if primary PCI is not possible within 120 minutes and mechanical complications are excluded; lysing and transferring are not exclusive.

**Dobutamine — low output without frank hypotension.** Dobutamine is a β₁ inotrope with β₂ vasodilation, so it raises output but can drop the blood pressure; it needs a pressure to start from. ESC also places an inotrope first in wet-cold patients with borderline pressure.

**Noradrenaline first, then add the inotrope.** Below SBP 90 (MAP <65) coronary and organ perfusion depend on pressure; noradrenaline raises it with less tachycardia and fewer arrhythmias than dopamine (SOAP II, worse outcome with dopamine in its cardiogenic subgroup) or adrenaline (OptimaCC: more refractory shock).

**Milrinone — PDE3 works downstream of the blocked β-receptor.** Milrinone inhibits phosphodiesterase III, so cAMP rises without needing the β-receptor; it also increases calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (lusitropy) and dilates veins and arteries, so it lowers the BP. Levosimendan also keeps working under β-blockade, by sensitising troponin C to calcium and opening K-ATP channels.

**Not routinely (IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit).** 30-day mortality 39.7% vs 41.3%, with no difference at 6 years. Of the devices, only the Impella CP has improved survival in STEMI shock (DanGer Shock: 180-day death 45.8% vs 58.5%), at the cost of more moderate or severe bleeding (21.8% vs 11.9%), limb ischaemia (5.6% vs 1.1%) and renal replacement (41.9% vs 26.7%) (CAR-26).
mimic: Milrinone vs levosimendan vs dobutamine

Dobutamine: β₁ agonist, blunted by β-blockers. Milrinone: PDE3, raises cAMP beyond the receptor. Levosimendan: calcium sensitiser, no cAMP. Both of the latter work in β-blocked patients and both vasodilate.
traps: “Lyse because the PCI centre is 3.5 h away”
With shock, transfer for revascularisation (only 9% right); ESC allows lysis as a bridge if PCI is beyond 120 min.
“Dopamine” as the inotrope for BP 80/50 in ADHF (DocT QBank key, 38%)
Outdated: dopamine caused more arrhythmias and deaths in cardiogenic shock (SOAP II). Noradrenaline for the pressure, dobutamine for the output.
“Start a vasopressor such as noradrenaline” for HFrEF at SBP 85 (DocT QBank keys dobutamine, 58%)
DocT follows ESC (inotrope first with borderline SBP); this card follows AHA/SCAI (noradrenaline below SBP 90). Low output with borderline SBP: dobutamine. Shock with MAP <65: noradrenaline first.
“Selective β₁ stimulation” or “troponin C sensitisation” for the drug that improves CO, venodilates and enhances SR calcium reuptake (GT2, 50%)
PDE3 inhibition, raising cAMP: milrinone.
decode: Large anterior STEMI, BP 72/40, rising lactate — intervention with the strongest survival impact? [DocT GT]
Early coronary reperfusion.
On dobutamine, BP keeps falling (85/55) [DocT QBank, 90%]
Add a vasopressor such as noradrenaline.
ADHF on chronic β-blocker, CO low despite high-dose dobutamine [DocT GT]
Levosimendan.
STEMI with shock, PCI centre door-to-balloon 75 min [DocT GT]
Primary PCI.
explain.punch: STEMI with shock goes for revascularisation of the culprit whatever the delay; dobutamine if the pressure holds, noradrenaline first if it does not, milrinone or levosimendan if β-blocked, and no routine IABP.

steps.q:
Inferior STEMI, BP 80/50, clear lungs,
raised JVP.
a Diagnosis and confirming lead
b First treatment
c Drugs to avoid
d If fluids fail
steps.a:
**RV infarction: preload-dependent — give**
**fluid, no nitrates**
a **RV infarction**; ST elevation in **V4R**.
b Cautious **crystalloid bolus** while arranging
primary PCI.
c **Nitrates, diuretics, morphine, β-blockers** —
all drop preload.
d **Dobutamine**; keep AV synchrony (pace if heart
block).

explain.intro: Not every infarct shock is a failing left ventricle. In an inferior STEMI with clear lungs and a high JVP, the right ventricle has stopped pushing, and the treatment is nearly the opposite of LV failure.
why: **RV infarction; ST elevation in V4R.** The right coronary artery usually supplies the RV; a proximal occlusion causes inferior STEMI with RV involvement. ST elevation ≥1 mm in V4R is the most sensitive ECG sign and fades within hours; echo shows a dilated, hypokinetic RV.

**Cautious crystalloid bolus while arranging primary PCI.** A stunned RV moves blood through the lungs only if it is filled at a higher pressure; without that the LV is underfilled and output falls. Fluid is given in small boluses, because an over-distended RV bulges the septum into the LV and lowers output again.

**Nitrates, diuretics, morphine, β-blockers — all drop preload.** Venodilation or diuresis removes the filling pressure the RV depends on; a sudden collapse after sublingual nitrate is the classic presentation.

**Dobutamine; keep AV synchrony (pace if heart block).** Inferior infarcts often cause AV block; losing atrial contraction removes a large part of RV filling, so sequential pacing helps more than ventricular pacing alone.
mimic: RV infarct vs LV cardiogenic shock
RV: clear lungs, high JVP, Kussmaul sign, preload-dependent, give fluid. LV: crackles, high PAWP, avoid fluid.
traps: “Medication-related adverse reaction” for collapse to 60/30 after nitrate in inferior STEMI
The nitrate unmasked a preload-dependent RV infarct: cardiogenic shock (46% right; the distractor also drew about 46%).
decode: Inferior STEMI given aspirin, nitrate and morphine; BP falls from 160/90 to 60/30 [DocT QBank, 46%]
Cardiogenic shock (RV infarction).
explain.punch: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, clear lungs and a high JVP is RV infarction: confirm with V4R, give cautious fluid, avoid nitrates, diuretics and morphine, use dobutamine and keep AV synchrony while PCI is arranged.

questions.text: Ruptures, aneurysm and the long road after

steps.q:
**For free wall, septal and papillary muscle rupture, give:**
a Presentation
b Key finding
c Management
d Surgical mortality
steps.a:
| **Free wall** | **VSR** | **Papillary**
**Presents** | Sudden pain + **collapse**, EMD | Rapid AHF / shock, **days 1-7** | Sudden pulmonary oedema ± shock
**Finding** | **Haemopericardium**, tamponade | **New loud systolic murmur** | Murmur (not always obvious); **posteromedial** muscle
**Manage** | Pericardiocentesis (bridge) → wall repair + patch | IABP bridge → surgery; percutaneous closure | Diuretic, vasodilator / inotrope ± IABP → MVR / repair
**Mortality** | **75-80%** | Early surgery **20-40%** | **20-25%**
- Free wall rupture: **<1%**; risk - older age, no reperfusion, **late lysis**

explain.intro: Step 5 is the most asked card in the deck (seven real questions). Necrotic muscle is softest before collagen is laid down, so the wall, septum or papillary muscle can tear in the first days to a week; the presentation and the echo tell you which, and the stem’s wording (‘next’ vs ‘definitive’) decides between a bridge and surgery.
why: **Presents: free wall — sudden pain + collapse, EMD; VSR — rapid AHF / shock, days 1–7; papillary — sudden pulmonary oedema ± shock.** Free wall rupture fills the pericardium in minutes, so the rhythm continues without output (PEA). VSR shunts left to right, flooding the lungs and starving the systemic circulation. Papillary rupture flails a mitral leaflet and the LV empties into a small, non-compliant left atrium.

**Finding: haemopericardium, tamponade; new loud systolic murmur (VSR); murmur not always obvious, posteromedial muscle (papillary).** The posteromedial muscle depends on one artery (the PDA, usually from the RCA), so it ruptures after inferior or posterior MI; the anterolateral has a dual supply. In acute MR the LA pressure rises so fast that the murmur may be short and soft, so a quiet heart with flash pulmonary oedema still means echo. Echo also shows the VSR jet, and a step-up in oxygen saturation from right atrium to pulmonary artery confirms the shunt.

**Manage: free wall — pericardiocentesis (bridge) → wall repair + patch; VSR — IABP bridge → surgery, percutaneous closure; papillary — diuretic, vasodilator / inotrope ± IABP → MVR / repair.** The IABP lowers afterload, which cuts the regurgitant and shunt fraction and raises forward flow without the extra afterload a vasopressor adds. Surgery is the definitive treatment for all three (ESC 2023: surgery preferred, IABP IIa, C while awaiting it; ACC/AHA 2025: short-term MCS as a bridge, 2a).

**Mortality: free wall 75–80%; VSR early surgery 20–40%; papillary 20–25%.** **Free wall rupture <1%; risk — older age, no reperfusion, late lysis.** For VSR the card’s figure is optimistic: registry operative mortality is about 54% when repair is within 7 days (MI-65). ESC 2023 puts all mechanical complications at 0.27% of STEMI with 42.4% in-hospital mortality; late lysis can turn an ischaemic infarct haemorrhagic and weaken it further.
mimic: VSR vs papillary muscle rupture
Both give a new systolic murmur and shock. VSR is loud with a thrill at the left sternal edge and an O₂ step-up; papillary MR is apical, often soft, with severe pulmonary oedema. Echo decides.
Free wall rupture vs post-MI pericarditis effusion
Rupture gives sudden tamponade and PEA; pericarditis gives a small effusion and pleuritic pain.
traps: “Norepinephrine” for inferior STEMI with a systolic murmur, pulmonary oedema and shock
Only 38% chose IABP. A pressor raises afterload and worsens the regurgitant flow; the IABP lowers afterload and supports coronary perfusion, and is IIa for mechanical complications.
“Valve replacement” as the ‘next’ step for papillary rupture with pulmonary oedema
Only 44% chose IABP. When IABP is offered and the stem says ‘next’, stabilise first; surgery is definitive.
“Diuretics and observe” or “vasodilator and reassess in 48 hours” for partial papillary rupture with hypotension
62% chose urgent mitral surgery. Without an IABP option, the answer is urgent surgery; medical therapy alone is fatal.
“Pulmonary embolism” or “LV systolic dysfunction” for dyspnoea with a new apical holosystolic murmur after posterior MI
69% chose acute MR; a new apical murmur with crackles and a preserved BP is papillary dysfunction until echo says otherwise.
decode: PEA / sudden hypotension days after a large STEMI, echo shows tamponade or haemopericardium — cause? [DocT GT ×2]
LV free wall rupture.
Post-MI flash pulmonary oedema, papillary muscle rupture on echo — next step? [DocT GT] [Marrow]
IABP if offered as the next step; otherwise urgent mitral repair/replacement.
Posterior MI with new apical holosystolic murmur and crackles — mechanism of dyspnoea? [DocT GT]
Acute mitral regurgitation.
Inferior STEMI, murmur, pulmonary oedema, cold and hypotensive — intervention? [DocT GT]
Intra-aortic balloon pump.
explain.punch: Sudden PEA with tamponade is free wall rupture; a new murmur with shock is VSR or papillary rupture, sorted by echo. Lower afterload with an IABP as the next step and send for surgery as the definitive one; avoid pressors that raise afterload.

steps.q:
**For ventricular septal rupture, give:**
a The infarcts it follows
b The early-surgery trade-off and indication
c The late-surgery trade-off and indication
d The newer option
steps.a:
- **Anterior** or **posterolateral** MI (per notes)
- High mortality (**20-40%**) - for **refractory** symptoms
- Risk of **rupture extension and death** while waiting - if **responding** to therapy
- **Percutaneous closure**

explain.intro: Step 5 narrowed to the septum. No real question is linked; the testable point is the timing trade-off — early surgery sews into friable necrotic muscle, late surgery risks death while waiting.
why: **Anterior or posterolateral MI (per notes).** Anterior MI (LAD) tears the apical septum, usually a simple defect; inferior MI (RCA/PDA) tears the basal inferior septum, a more complex defect often with RV infarction and a worse outcome. The usual pairing in guidelines and reviews is anterior and inferior.

**Early surgery: high mortality (20–40%) — for refractory symptoms.** The necrotic edges hold sutures poorly before scar forms, so early repair carries higher mortality and residual leaks; a patient in refractory shock has no other option. The card’s figure is low: in the STS registry operative mortality was 54% when repair was within 7 days of MI and 18% after that, partly because the sickest are operated on first.

**Late surgery: risk of rupture extension and death while waiting — if responding to therapy.** Delaying lets the edges fibrose and improves repair, but the defect can enlarge; this route is only for those stable on IABP or MCS and drugs.
**Percutaneous closure.** A septal occluder device, used in selected anatomy, as a bridge or for residual defects after surgery.
mimic: Apical (anterior MI) vs basal (inferior MI) VSR
Apical is simpler to repair; basal is complex and carries a worse prognosis.
traps: “Wait 4–6 weeks for every VSR”
Only if the patient is stable; in refractory shock operate now despite the risk.
decode: Post-MI VSR in refractory shock despite IABP — timing of surgery? [pattern]
Emergency surgery.
Post-MI VSR stable on support — strategy? [pattern]
Delayed surgery (or percutaneous closure) once the edges have scarred.
explain.punch: Early VSR repair is a dangerous operation on soft tissue and is reserved for those who cannot wait; delayed repair is safer for the stable, provided the defect does not extend.

steps.q:
**For post-MI LV aneurysm, give:**
a Incidence and usual site
b The two ECG features
c The main complication and its treatment
d Indications for surgery
steps.a:
- **<5%** of AMI; **anteroseptal / apical** LV
- **Persistent ST elevation**; **Q waves**
- **LV thrombus** (apex) → systemic embolism → **long-term oral anticoagulation**
- Large aneurysm, **recurrent thromboembolism**, mural / apical thrombus

explain.intro: Step 5 at the slow end. Instead of tearing, a transmural scar can thin and bulge, and it shows on the ECG as an ST elevation that never settles. The one real question (46% right) tests the Q wave, the permanent part of the scar.
why: **<5% of AMI; anteroseptal / apical LV.** Large anterior transmural infarcts without timely reperfusion; with prompt PCI aneurysm has become uncommon.

**Persistent ST elevation; Q waves.** The akinetic scar keeps the ST segment raised for weeks after the event, and the dead myocardium leaves Q waves. With no new pain and no new troponin rise, this is a fixed scar, not a new infarct (MI-27).

**LV thrombus (apex) → systemic embolism → long-term oral anticoagulation.** Stasis in the akinetic apex forms thrombus (over 9% after anterior STEMI). ESC 2023 says OAC (warfarin or a NOAC) ‘should be considered for 3–6 months’, guided by repeat echo or CMR, rather than indefinitely.
**Large aneurysm, recurrent thromboembolism, mural / apical thrombus.** Aneurysmectomy is also considered for refractory heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias arising from the aneurysm.
mimic: True aneurysm vs pseudoaneurysm

A true aneurysm is a wide-necked bulge of scar that rarely ruptures; a pseudoaneurysm is a contained free wall rupture with a narrow neck, walled by pericardium, and needs surgery because it ruptures.
Old MI vs acute MI on ECG
Q waves without ST elevation mean an old, healed infarct; ST elevation with symptoms or rising troponin is acute; persistent ST elevation with Q waves weeks later is aneurysm.
traps: “Acute coronary syndrome” for Q waves in I, aVL and V5 with exertional dyspnoea
Only 46% chose old MI. Q waves are permanent scar; acute ischaemia needs ST or T changes and a matching story.
“Re-infarction — reperfuse” for ST elevation weeks after an anterior MI
Persistent ST elevation with deep Q waves and no new troponin rise is aneurysm.
decode: Known CAD, fatigue, ECG with Q waves in I, aVL, V5 — diagnosis? [DocT QBank]
Old (lateral) myocardial infarction.
ST elevation still present 6 weeks after an anterior MI — cause? [pattern]
LV aneurysm.
explain.punch: Persistent ST elevation with Q waves weeks after an anterior MI is an aneurysm, not a new infarct; its danger is apical thrombus and embolism, treated with oral anticoagulation (ESC: 3–6 months), and surgery is for the large or embolising aneurysm.

parts.q: What makes a Q wave pathological? [DocT QBank]
parts.a: The classic definition is at least 40 ms wide or deeper than 25% of the following R wave, in two or more contiguous leads. The Fourth Universal Definition uses a lower bar: Q ≥30 ms and ≥1 mm deep (in V2–V3, any Q over 20 ms or a QS complex) in two contiguous leads.

steps.q:
**For long-term drugs after MI (ESC strategy figures), give the class by LVEF:**
a Oral beta-blocker
b ACE inhibitor
c MRA
d Statin
e DAPT
steps.a:
**Drug** | **LVEF **≤**40% or HF** | **LVEF >40%**
**Oral β-blocker** | **I, A** | IIa, B (figure)
**ACE inhibitor** | **I, A** | IIa, A (no HF)
**MRA** | **I, B** - LVEF ≤40% AND HF | -

explain.intro: Step 6: what the patient takes for life. The one real question (47% right) asks which drug improves prognosis in post-MI HFrEF; the card sorts every drug by LVEF so the answer drops out.
why: **Oral beta-blocker: I, A if LVEF ≤40% or HF; IIa, B if LVEF >40%.** Blocking catecholamines lowers oxygen demand, raises the VF threshold and lets the remodelling ventricle recover; with low LVEF the old trials cut death by over 20%. Above 40% the evidence is now split: REDUCE-AMI (LVEF ≥50%) and REBOOT (LVEF >40%) showed no overall benefit, BETAMI-DANBLOCK (LVEF ≥40%) showed fewer events (HR 0.85, mainly fewer reinfarctions, with no difference in death), and a pooled analysis of LVEF 40–49% (n 1,885) cut death, MI or HF from 14.4% to 10.7% (HR 0.75). So the case is strong at ≤49% and weak at ≥50% (MI-73).

**ACE inhibitor: I, A if LVEF ≤40% or HF (also diabetes, hypertension, CKD); IIa, A in all others.** ACE inhibition limits angiotensin-driven dilatation and fibrosis of the infarcted ventricle; an ARB (valsartan, VALIANT) is the alternative if intolerant.

**MRA: I, B — LVEF ≤40% AND HF (or diabetes).** ESC 2023 now grades this I, A (LVEF ≤40% with HF or diabetes). Aldosterone drives fibrosis and potassium loss despite an ACE inhibitor; eplerenone in EPHESUS cut death and CV admissions in exactly this group. Check potassium and creatinine first.

**High-dose statin: I, A — all.** Given regardless of LVEF or baseline cholesterol, as early as possible; ESC targets LDL-C <1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) and a 50% fall, adding ezetimibe then a PCSK9 inhibitor if needed.
**DAPT: 12 months — all.** Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (prasugrel or ticagrelor preferred) by default for 12 months, shortened for high bleeding risk (CVS10C).
mimic: Prognostic drugs vs symptomatic drugs in post-MI HFrEF
Beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARNI, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor prolong life; nitrates, digoxin and diuretics relieve symptoms only.
traps: “Intravenous milrinone” for an EF of 25% with dyspnoea
Only 47% chose the beta-blocker. Inotropes raise oxygen demand and arrhythmias and increase long-term mortality; they are a bridge in shock, not prognostic therapy.
“Digoxin” or “nitrates” to improve prognosis
Digoxin reduced HF admissions but not death (DIG); nitrates treat angina only.
“Beta-blocker is Class I for every post-MI patient”
Only for LVEF ≤40%; above that ESC gives IIa and the newest trials disagree.
decode: Post-MI, EF 25%, stable but breathless — which therapy improves long-term prognosis? [DocT QBank]
Oral beta-blocker (the only prognostic option offered).
Post-MI, LVEF 35% with HF on ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker — what to add? [pattern]
An MRA (eplerenone/spironolactone).
explain.punch: Everyone gets a high-dose statin and 12 months of DAPT; LVEF ≤40% adds a beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor as Class I, and an MRA if there is HF. Inotropes, digoxin and nitrates never improve prognosis.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Beta-blockers after MI without reduced EF
explain.intro: Step 6 starts with the drug whose old rule (everyone after MI) came from the pre-reperfusion era. No real question is linked; four recent trials answer whether reperfused patients with good LVEF still need it.
why: **REDUCE-AMI: LVEF ≥50% → no benefit.** 5,020 patients with obstructive CAD, 95% treated by PCI: death or MI 7.9% vs 8.3% (HR 0.96) over a median 3.5 years. With a small infarct and a normal ventricle there is little arrhythmic or remodelling substrate for the drug to act on.

**REBOOT (~8,000): LVEF >40%, no HF → no benefit overall; signal at 40–49%.** 8,505 patients: death, reinfarction or HF admission HR 1.04 (0.89–1.22). A prespecified sex analysis suggested more events with beta-blockers in women, mainly those with preserved EF, and none in men; it is hypothesis-generating, not a reason to withhold the drug when LVEF is reduced.

**BETAMI-DANBLOCK (~5,500): LVEF ≥40% → fewer events (14.2% vs 16.3%).** 5,574 patients, HR 0.85 (0.75–0.98), median follow-up about 3.5 years. Unlike REDUCE-AMI it included patients with mildly reduced EF (40–49%), where the benefit is concentrated; like the other trials it was open-label.

**LVEF 40–49% (4 trials) → 25% relative reduction in death / MI / HF (10.7% vs 14.4%).** The pooled analysis of 1,885 patients with mildly reduced EF from REBOOT, BETAMI, DANBLOCK and CAPITAL-RCT gave HR 0.75 (0.58–0.97). The benefit lies where the ventricle is damaged; it fades as LVEF normalises.
mimic: Starting vs stopping

REDUCE-AMI and REBOOT ask whether to start after a reperfused MI with good LVEF; ABYSS asks whether to stop years later: interruption (LVEF ≥40%, MI a median 2.9 years before) failed non-inferiority (23.8% vs 21.1%), mostly CV admissions, with no quality-of-life gain.
traps: “A long-term beta-blocker improves outcome in every post-MI patient”

Proven long-term benefit is for LVEF ≤40% (I, A in both guidelines) and, from the 2025 pooled data, 40–49%; at LVEF ≥50% REDUCE-AMI and REBOOT show none. The guidelines predate REBOOT: ESC 2023 gives routine beta-blockers regardless of LVEF IIa, and ACC/AHA 2025 still advises starting an oral beta-blocker within 24 hours in all ACS without contraindications (1, A), mainly against reinfarction and arrhythmia, leaving the duration in preserved EF open.
decode: [pattern] Reperfused STEMI, LVEF 58%, no HF — does a long-term beta-blocker improve outcome?
No clear benefit (REDUCE-AMI, REBOOT).
[pattern] Post-MI LVEF 45% — beta-blocker?
Yes: mildly reduced EF benefits (pooled analysis, HR 0.75).
explain.punch: After a reperfused MI the beta-blocker earns its place when LVEF is below 50% and has no proven benefit when LVEF is preserved; stopping one years later has not been shown to be safe (ABYSS).

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Lipids, rehabilitation and anaemia (ACC/AHA 2025)
explain.intro: Step 6 ends with the long-term prescriptions. No real question is linked; the testable points are the two LDL thresholds with different classes and the haemoglobin of 10.
why: **High-intensity statin for all.** 1, A, regardless of baseline LDL-C (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg), because the benefit tracks the absolute LDL-C reduction and ACS patients are at the highest risk.

**LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL → add ezetimibe / PCSK9 inhibitor / inclisiran / bempedoic acid (I).** 1, A on a maximally tolerated statin; each further fall in LDL-C lowers events (IMPROVE-IT, FOURIER, ODYSSEY OUTCOMES).

**LDL-C 55–69 mg/dL (IIa).** 2a, B-R. 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) is the ESC goal, so the American guideline has moved towards it without making it a mandate. The ESC 2025 focused update keeps the goals and adds earlier combination: intensify during the index admission if already treated (I, C); start statin plus ezetimibe in hospital if the goal looks unreachable with statin alone (IIa, B).
**Fasting panel at 4–8 weeks after starting or changing therapy.** 1, C-LD: by then the statin effect is complete, so the result decides whether to add a non-statin agent.

**Refer before discharge (I); home-based if centre unavailable.** Referral before discharge is 1, A, because patients referred later often never attend; home-based rehabilitation is a reasonable alternative (2a).

**Transfusion to maintain Hb 10 g/dL may be reasonable.** 2b, B-R in ACS with anaemia and no active bleeding. Anaemia lowers oxygen delivery to an ischaemic myocardium; in MINT, a liberal target (≥10 g/dL) gave fewer 30-day deaths or MIs than restrictive (7–8 g/dL), 14.5% vs 16.9% (RR 1.15 for restrictive, P 0.07), so the difference fell short of significance and the class is only 2b. This is an exception to the general ICU threshold of 7 g/dL, which was never tested in acute MI.
mimic: Hb threshold: ACS vs general ICU
ACS with anaemia: aiming for 10 g/dL may be reasonable (MINT). General ICU: transfuse below 7 g/dL (TRICC).
traps: “LDL-C 60 mg/dL on maximal statin: adding ezetimibe is Class 1”
55–69 mg/dL is 2a (reasonable); Class 1 begins at ≥70 mg/dL (watch line).
“Restrictive transfusion (Hb 7) in acute MI with anaemia”
ACS is the exception: Hb 10 g/dL may be reasonable.
decode: [pattern] Post-ACS on atorvastatin 80 mg, LDL-C 82 mg/dL — next step?
Add a non-statin agent (1, A).
[pattern] NSTEMI, Hb 8.2 g/dL, no bleeding — transfusion target?
Hb 10 g/dL may be reasonable (2b, MINT).
explain.punch: High-intensity statin for all, add a non-statin agent at LDL-C ≥70 (Class 1) and consider one at 55–69 (2a), recheck at 4–8 weeks, refer to rehab before discharge, and in ACS anaemia aim for Hb 10, not 7.
